title: Clarify third edition documentation about warnings
description:
I'm currently migrating my package testing to use `testthat`'s third edition and I'm very excited to use all those awesome-looking features.

However, the greatest issue I'm facing so far is that warnings are now limited to one output only, which leads to quite an intense refactoring in my code (but perhaps it is a hint it was flawed in the first place).

Since it has been described as a feature and not a bug in https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/1255, I guess it is a matter of documentation.

First, it would be nice if this change could be mentioned in https://testthat.r-lib.org/articles/third-edition.html#changes, as this is most likely the first place one may start to learn how to migrate. 

Also, in https://testthat.r-lib.org/reference/expect_snapshot.html, the case of warnings is not crystal-clear. You have to read the help up to the `class` argument to figure out that `expect_snapshot_error()` can accept warnings. 

But most importantly, the naming is quite surprising: 

> `expect_snapshot_error()` captures just error messages.

Warnings and messages are not usually considered errors, so one would not expect to catch them with this function. Also, since errors can have classes, I found it further surprising to say that warnings are of some subclass of error. 

I would rather have expected something like `expect_snapshot_condition(x, type=c("error", "warning", "message"), class=NULL, cran=FALSE)`, with `class` to catch some specific subclass of error/warning, best along with handy helpers like `expect_snapshot_error()`, `expect_snapshot_warning()`, and `expect_snapshot_message()`.

In addition, note that `expect_snapshot()` comes with a `error=FALSE` option, but not with a `warning=FALSE` option. If this is not a feature you would consider adding, it would be nice to describe there how this function is meant to behave regarding warnings.

Finally, in https://testthat.r-lib.org/reference/expect_error.html, the "In the 3rd edition" mention is not very obvious, shouldn't it be in a specific section, or in bold at least?

Thanks again for your incredible work.

title: testing packages has too many colors in terminal output
description:
My test iteration process is quite normal I think:

 * do some coding
 * run tests
 * and then depending on how long the testing takes:
   * wait to observe results or...
   * go back to code and look back at test results

My terminal looks like this when I test (Rtest is just an alias to run devtools::test() )

![Screenshot from 2021-05-23 13-31-27](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4111/119258779-7c1d9200-bbcb-11eb-9970-1fad755b6185.png)

Glancing back to this terminal, from my IDE, there's a lot to take in, when all I'm interested in is wheter or not there were test failures. (One does get the feeling that whomever coded the terminal testoutput thought terminal colors were a terrific hammer)

* Colors are a strong visual aid. However the colors in the test output are _non-informative_ to the test result, they are decribing generic sections, not specific results.
* The test specfic bits of the output is white text (the numbers of test outcomes), which is the last thing my brain sees.
In this case:

* Orange FAIL hits my eyesight first, giving the initial interpration that there are test failures here.
* The brain then remembers not to get alarmed by alarming colors, and starts looking for more info.
* It spends some extra energy not getting caught up by lines and structure leading it to where it shouldn't be lead.
* Eyes then doesn't easily see the "0" next ot FAIL, but instead finds the magenta WARN that draws my eyes to itself.
* At this point the 0's next to both FAIL and WARN start to get noticed, and I feel reassured and but search on for the PASS number all at the end of the line, with a reassuringly high number next ot it.
* Also the double lines lead my eyes to see above it for what goes on, when the first thing I want to see is the test fail count. This can perhaps be learned. Though I have been testing packages for many years. If you fix the colors, I am inclined to accept or rewire brain for the double line.

## I propose:

* Use the colors to indidcate _specific result_, not _generic function_:
  * When there are test failures, only hightlight FAIL with red
  * When there are no test failures, only highlight PASS with green.

In a busy everyday life with rapidly approaching deadlines, this would make this one less thing to spend extra energy on.

Yes, I could perhaps tune my terminal colors, but I won't do that for thet sole purpose of accomodating R testoutput (not yet atleast)

Also if I only worked with R and only ever used TDD with R packages in my everyday life, I would get acustomed to the specific quirks of its test output. But I don't, I would guess most poeple don't. There are all kinds of systems, languages and platofrm, each of course will do things their own way,

title: testhat removes environment when run interactivelly but not when from CMD check
description:
Hi, I have a package that contains a compiled JAGS module and needs to load it in order to function. I managed to make it working on github actions and when running with `check()`, however, the unit tests fail on `test()`.

The issue is that `on.load()` I assign location of the compiled dll to a package's environment:
```
  modloc <- gsub('/$','', file.path(libname, pkgname, 'libs', if(.Platform$r_arch!="") .Platform$r_arch else ""))
  if(!file.exists(file.path(modloc, paste('RoBMA', .Platform$dynlib.ext, sep='')))){
    modloc <- ''
    warning('The RoBMA module could not be loaded.', call. =FALSE)
  }else{
    rjags::load.module("RoBMA", path = modloc)
    library.dynam("RoBMA", "RoBMA", libname)
    RoBMA.private$modulelocation <- modloc
  }
```

When I run the tests via `check()`, I do not notice any issues, but when running with `test()` the `RoBMA.private$modulelocation` becomes `NULL` and the module can't be loaded.

I checked that I can circumvent the issue locally by adding `setup.R` file that loads the module with a hardcoded location, but that's far from an ideal solution. 

(I apologize in advance if I omitted any important detail but I'm not an expert on compiled code and how to link it, so I'm not sure how to properly described it, the repo if it is helpful is here: https://github.com/FBartos/RoBMA/tree/pre-release)

Cheers,
Frantisek

title: Add expect_predicate() for chainable inspection?
description:
In the course of writing up this issue, I've realized that [`magrittr`'s "tee" pipe](https://magrittr.tidyverse.org/reference/tee.html) is a good candidate for this, but since `testthat` doesn't re-export this function (nor am I convinced that it necessarily should), I figured I'd float this idea anyway.

In the unit tests for a function I'm working on, I want to ensure that an object is an array, along with some other assertions. To chain these assertions, I used the pipe operator, as alluded to by `testthat`'s documentation. It looked something like the below.

```R
f(x) %>%
  {expect_true(is.array(.))} %>%
  custom_expectation()
```

When running the test, my custom expectation kept failing, which was bewildering, since it definitely held in interactive inspection. Eventually, it dawned on me that the custom expectation was being passed `is.array(f(x))` instead of `f(x)` itself. It's perfectly clear to me now why this is the case, but I spent some time very confused.

To help overcome this, I'm wondering if it might be suitable to introduce an expectation, something like `expect_predicate()`, which could evaluate a predicate for truth, returning *the original object* instead of `TRUE`/`FALSE`. This would enable chains where multiple orthogonal object properties are investigated while retaining the use of the "normal" pipe `%>%`:

```R
f(x) %>%
  expect_predicate(!is.null(.$a)) %>%
  expect_predicate(.$b > 0) %>%
  expect_class("f")
```

I believe the second form above might require some metaprogramming to pull off properly.

If this is something that's deemed potentially of interest, I'd be happy to write up a PR (and/or proof-of-concept for trying it out), but I figured I'd open this issue before doing so.

title: testthat removes active bindings
description:
My package uses an active binding to provide a global pronoun that has a context-dependent value. It seems that when testing a package, `testthat` will clone the package environment which turns the active bindings into frozen values. I can still make my tests pass by prefixing the active bindings with  explicit package namespace, but this behavior definitely seems unexpected. 

Here is a quick example (using a mock package `active_binding_test`):

```r
#' @export active_binding
makeActiveBinding("active_binding", function() value, environment())

value <- NULL

#' @export
set_value <- function(x) value <<- x
```

and the test:

```r
# this will fail
test_that("active_binding works correctly", {
  set_value("a value")
  expect_identical(active_binding, "a value")
})

# this will succeed
test_that("active_binding_test::active_binding works correctly", {
  set_value("another value")
  expect_identical(active_binding_test::active_binding, "another value")
})
```

title: expect_snapshot_value() fails with various errors with complex objects
description:
My package is outputting MS Word documents and I've been wanting to test their reproducibility for ages. 

Third edition's snapshots are the perfect solution for that.

Obviouly, as a raw `docx` file is tracking a bunch of things that make it unreproducible (mostly dates and paths), `expect_snapshot_file()` will unfortunately not be usable in this case.

However, the `docx` object that allowed to save such a file is a plain R object that should be snapshotable.

Here is a reprex of comparability:

``` r
library(testthat)
library(officer)

#remove all non-reproducible internals
clean_docx = function(x){
    x$package_dir = "test"
    x$content_type$.__enclos_env__$private$filename = "test"
    x$doc_obj$.__enclos_env__$private$filename = "test"
    x$doc_obj$.__enclos_env__$private$package_dir = "test"
    x$doc_obj$.__enclos_env__$private$rels_filename = "test"
    x$footnotes$.__enclos_env__$private$filename = "test"
    x$footnotes$.__enclos_env__$private$package_dir = "test"
    x$footnotes$.__enclos_env__$private$rels_filename = "test"
    x
}

x=read_docx() %>% body_add_par("This is a test")
y=read_docx() %>% body_add_par("This is a test")

all.equal(x, y)
#> [1] "Component \"package_dir\": 1 string mismatch"                                                                                 
#> [2] "Component \"content_type\": Component \".__enclos_env__\": Component \"private\": Component \"filename\": 1 string mismatch"  
#> [3] "Component \"doc_obj\": Component \".__enclos_env__\": Component \"private\": Component \"filename\": 1 string mismatch"       
#> [4] "Component \"doc_obj\": Component \".__enclos_env__\": Component \"private\": Component \"package_dir\": 1 string mismatch"    
#> [5] "Component \"doc_obj\": Component \".__enclos_env__\": Component \"private\": Component \"rels_filename\": 1 string mismatch"  
#> [6] "Component \"footnotes\": Component \".__enclos_env__\": Component \"private\": Component \"filename\": 1 string mismatch"     
#> [7] "Component \"footnotes\": Component \".__enclos_env__\": Component \"private\": Component \"package_dir\": 1 string mismatch"  
#> [8] "Component \"footnotes\": Component \".__enclos_env__\": Component \"private\": Component \"rels_filename\": 1 string mismatch"
digest::digest(x)
#> [1] "95ae71952dcd2e3e7193785497523067"
digest::digest(y)
#> [1] "01f83d7fa2c6694f182dd537be5c9d6a"

x=read_docx() %>% body_add_par("This is a test") %>% clean_docx()
y=read_docx() %>% body_add_par("This is a test") %>% clean_docx()

all.equal(x, y)
#> [1] TRUE
digest::digest(x)
#> [1] "afb5e4f2db88b14df514097cdd4599a1"
digest::digest(y)
#> [1] "afb5e4f2db88b14df514097cdd4599a1"
```

<sup>Created on 2021-02-28 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>



Unfortunately, this test (which should be reproducible) will fail with various error messages:

```r
library(officer)
test_that("word document", {
    local_edition(3)
    doc = read_docx() %>% 
        body_add_par("This is a test") %>% 
        clean_docx()
    
    expect_snapshot_value(doc, style = "json")
    #expect_snapshot_value(doc, style = "json2")
    #expect_snapshot_value(doc, style = "serialize")
})
```

With `json`, I get the error: "Error: No method asJSON S3 class: rdocx". (seems legit)  
With `json2`, I get the error: "Error: attempt to apply non-function".   
With `serialize`, I get the error: "Error: external pointer is not valid".

Also, would you consider allowing to use `digest::digest()` as an `expect_snapshot_value()` `style`? They are both unreadable but the former being shorter, it might be easier to compare and the output would be much less clumsy.   
Even better, you might want to consider letting the user choose any function, but that might require a hard work of abstraction that might not be relevant.

Side note, it seems that `serialize()` uses the R version ([link](https://stackoverflow.com/a/41876840/3888000)) which might lead to some unreproducibility if a file is compared to a snapshot that was created right before an R upgrade.

When comparing data.frames, I would like to ignore row names as I will be comparing different parts of the data.frames against each other. title: Custom comparison function for `expect_snapshot_file()`
description:
I have been struggling a bit with trying to get some tests on plot outputs to pass on gh action runs. With a bit of trial and error, I believe I managed to get both my local machine and the actions VM produce images that are identical on a pixel level, however non-identical wrt the current [comparison function](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/e3cb86d8332238ad9bd2d760a52c7a7edcfecada/R/snapshot-file.R#L188-L192)

```r
compare_file_binary <- function(old, new) {
  old <- brio::read_file_raw(old)
  new <- brio::read_file_raw(new)
  identical(old, new)
}
```

A potentially worthwhile addition to the `expect_snapshot_file()` API could be an argument for specifying a custom comparison function. For my use-case for example

```r
compare_img_data <- function(old, new) {
  old <- magick::image_read(old)
  new <- magick::image_read(new)
  identical(magick::image_data(new), magick::image_data(old))
}
```

would do the trick. This could make `expect_snapshot_file()` much more powerful than it currently is. For example, again using the magick package, a user could test for image similarity by thresholding the result of `magick::image_compare_dist()`, etc.

My suggestion would be to add a minor change to [`expect_snapshot_file()`](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/e3cb86d8332238ad9bd2d760a52c7a7edcfecada/R/snapshot-file.R#L56-L81), something along the lines of https://github.com/nbenn/testthat/commit/9f91064703ff75eb08e6ec44295468c1f4c7a6fd. I'm happy to expand this to a proper PR if this is of interest to others as well.

title: auto-deletion of snapshots on devtools::test() has false positives on test failures
description:
(not sure if this is a testthat or vdiffr issue, but I am 95% sure it is testthat, so posting here but tagging @lionel-)

I encountered a snag in my workflow while trying out the new workflow for vdiffr that is based on snapshots, and I am wondering if I've missed a more sensible workflow or if devtools::test() is being a bit too trigger-happy on deleting unused snapshots.

Basically, while fixing some bugs in {ggdist} (which has a large number of vdiffr test cases), I've discovered that if there is a bug in a test case that causes a snapshot to fail (e.g. a bug that causes `vdiffr::expect_doppelganger()` to error), if you run `devtools::test()` it will think that the corresponding snapshot is no longer used and delete it (I provide an example below). I think this is somewhat problematic because once you fix the bug causing the error, the snapshot to test against is no longer there! 

You can kind of work around this by filtering to specific files (which seems not to delete unused test cases), but this is still cumbersome because: (1) often (if you're like me) you'll discover the bug by running `devtools::test()`, so the test case is already deleted and (2) I'd much prefer to be able to have fast enough test cases that I can reflexively run the full suite while fixing stuff, especially if there are lots of test cases or problems in multiple parts of the package introduced by a change in an upstream dep.

## An example

Create a package, run `usethis::use_testthat()`, then add this test file:

```r
library(ggplot2)

test_that("simple plot", {
  vdiffr::expect_doppelganger("simple plot", ggplot(data.frame(), aes(1,1)) + geom_point())
})
```

Running `devtools::test()` the first time creates the snapshot:

```
i Loading testpkg
i Testing testpkg
√ |  OK F W S | Context
√ |   1   1   | test [0.1 s]                                                                              
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Warning (test-test.R:4:3): simple plot
Adding new file snapshot: '_snaps/test/simple-plot.svg'
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```

Second run of `devtools::test()` passes:

```
i Loading testpkg
i Testing testpkg
√ |  OK F W S | Context
√ |   1       | test                                                                                      

== Results ===============================================================================================
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 1 ]
```

Now imagine the above test started erroring. Simulate that by changing the test case to use `stop()`:

```r
library(ggplot2)

test_that("simple plot", {
  vdiffr::expect_doppelganger("simple plot", stop())
})
```

Run `devtools::test()` again, and the snapshot is deleted:

```
i Loading testpkg
i Testing testpkg
√ |  OK F W S | Context
x |   0 1     | test                                                                                      
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Error (test-test.R:4:3): simple plot
Error: 
Backtrace:
 1. vdiffr::expect_doppelganger("simple plot", stop()) test-test.R:4:2
 2. vdiffr:::writer(fig, testcase, title)
 3. vdiffr:::print_plot(plot, title)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

== Results ===============================================================================================
[ FAIL 1 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 0 ]
Deleting unused snapshots:
* _snaps/test/simple-plot.svg
```

Now if I fix that test case, I won't have the old snapshot to compare against. I can restore it from git, but this is cumbersome (especially if this happens with several test cases).

## Expected behavior

I'm not sure the best behavior, but I don't recall encountering problems like this with the old `devtools::test()` followed by `vdiffr::manage_cases()` workflow, which seemed to correctly identify orphaned test cases without ever accidentally deleting stuff.

title: Tracebacks when piping into an expectation
description:
I've noticed that when piping into an expectation a failed test always comes with a traceback even in situations where it seems like one isn't warranted.

For example,
```
f = function(x) x
test_that("testing", {
  f(1) %>% expect_equal(2)
})
```
yields a traceback where this doesn't output one:
```
f = function(x) x
test_that("testing", {
   expect_equal(f(1), 2)
})
```

Is this expected?/Is there a way to turn off the traceback in this situation?

Thanks!

title: Tests skip_on_cran are skipped with (local) R CMD check
description:
I have noticed that in case the package is checked with `R CMD check` locally (so not on CRAN), the tests containing `skip_on_cran` are skipped.

The issue seems to be due to the fact that if the variable `NOT_CRAN` is NOT set, `skip_on_cran` will return TRUE (as not identical to 'true', see this [line](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/skip.R#L131)).

Thanks in advance for feedback!

title: Support setting the value of testthat edition via an environment variable
description:
Hi team!

I hope this finds you well, and thanks for all of the great work on `testthat`.

We use a build system to support R at Google, which unfortunately makes it somewhat difficult to access a package's description file when running tests. Instead, we've modified `testthat` internally to be able to set the edition using an environment variable.

Is this something worth supporting for other users?

Thanks!

description:
Hi,

[1] 4070365163

Test passed 😀

[1] 18842168632
> testthat::test_that('a', {testthat::expect_equal(1, 1)})
Test passed 🌈

[1] 18842168634
```
Note that `sum(.Random.seed)` increases by `1` after each subsequent run of `test_that()`. Is this an expected behaviour?

title: Wrong specification of regexp in `snap_from_md`
description:
In this line: https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/snapshot-serialize.R#L19, the regexp is specified as `grepl("^-{3, }", ...)`. Note that there is a space in front of } which is, according to the regex documentation, wrong. For an unknown reason, R accepts this specification, but throws an error in this case `grepl("^-{3, 5}, ...)`. If you try to use the pattern `^-{3, }`, it should match this string "-{3, }". R wrongly ignores the space there.

The correct pattern should be "^-{3,}".

title: Clarification of documentation of 'exact' argument in 'expect_s3_class'
description:
I'm currently writing tests for a package in which I test multiple classes of an object.

`expect_s3_class` has the argument `class` which can be a character vector of class names.  When I test my object against a vector of classes, it still passes even if one of them isn't valid.  This is expected behaviour, and can be resolved by using the `exact` argument, as discussed in #885.  

```
x <- data.frame(x = 1:10, y = "x", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)

# Success
expect_s3_class(x, c("data.frame", "made_up_class"))

# Failure
expect_s3_class(x, c("data.frame", "made_up_class"), exact = TRUE)
```

However, the way that the `exact` argument works when the `class` argument is a character vector isn't completely clear from the documentation.

The documentation for the `exact` argument reads "If FALSE, the default, checks that object inherits from class. If TRUE, checks that object has a class that's identical to class."

I'd like to propose that it's rephrased to something like "If FALSE, the default, checks that object inherits from at least one of the vector of classes. If TRUE, checks that object has a class or classes that are identical to class."

title: expect_equal breaks up vctrs records
description:
`testthat::expect_equal()` appears to "break up" [vctrs records](https://vctrs.r-lib.org/reference/new_vctr.html).

I've observed a similar (related?) behavior in purrr https://github.com/tidyverse/purrr/issues/819.

Crucially, `testthat::expect_equal()` *does* otherwise respect equalities set by [`vctrs::vec_proxy_equal()`](https://vctrs.r-lib.org/reference/vec_proxy_equal.html).

This just affects records, AFAIK, and, as per the output, it's natural that it would happen, because testthat (or waldo?) seems to compare the record *fields* as opposed to the entire record.

Apologies:
- the reprex ain't short; unfortunately setting up a record takes a bit, including a format method.
    This is from the vignette.
- I'm not sure whether this belongs in testthat or vctrs.

``` r
library(vctrs)
library(testthat)
new_rational <- function(n = integer(), d = integer()) {
  # assertions from vignette dropped
  new_rcrd(list(n = n, d = d), class = "vctrs_rational")
}

format.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) {
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")

  out <- paste0(n, "/", d)
  out[is.na(n) | is.na(d)] <- NA

  out
}

gcd <- function(x, y) {
  r <- x %% y
  ifelse(r, gcd(y, r), y)
}

vec_proxy_equal.vctrs_rational <- function(x, ...) {
  n <- field(x, "n")
  d <- field(x, "d")
  gcd <- gcd(n, d)

  data.frame(n = n / gcd, d = d / gcd)
}

# works now
new_rational(1, 1) == new_rational(2, 2)
#> [1] TRUE

# but testthat does not respect this
test_that("Rationals can be compared", {
  expect_equal(new_rational(1, 1), new_rational(2, 2))
})
#> ── Failure (<text>:36:3): Rationals can be compared ────────────────────────────
#> new_rational(1, 1) not equal to new_rational(2, 2).
#> Component "n": Mean relative difference: 1
#> Component "d": Mean relative difference: 1
```

title: Global variables are not passed into parallel tests
description:
I'm trying to upgrade to the third edition of testthat to leverage the parallel test capabilities, but the globals I define in my setup file are not getting passed into the individual test threads. When I run the tests with a single thread using test_file everything passes, but when I use parallel tests (even with TESTTHAT_CPUS=1) the single thread does not see the globals defined in my setup file.

Is the difference in behavior between the two ways of executing tests working as designed or is it a bug?

title: `auto_test_package()` package is not a string
description:
## Overview
After the first run of `auto_test_package()` (i.e., when it had actually started to acting automatically), when a test changes, an error is returned:
```
Error: package is not a string
```




## Step to reproduce the problem

```
usethis::create_package("foo")
usethis::use_test("foo")
testthat::auto_test_package()  # everything works up to here
# make and save any change to test-foo.R
# "Error: package is not a string"
```




## TL;DR (proposed solution)

The `test_files` call inside the `watcher` function defined into `auto_test_package` ([auto-test.R#L43](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/auto-test.R#L43)) could be wrong:

it is `test_files(tests, env, reporter = reporter$clone(deep = TRUE))` while I think it should be:

```
test_files(
        test_dir = test_path,
        test_package = package,
        test_paths = tests,
        env = env,
        reporter = reporter$clone(deep = TRUE)
)
```

Let me know if you agree with the solution and like a pull-request.








## Details
Unfortunately, stopping the automation and calling `traceback()` is not that much informative:

```
3. Sys.sleep(1) at watcher.R#23
2. watch(c(code_path, test_path), watcher, hash = hash) at auto-test.R#132
1. auto_test_package() 
```

After some investigations, I (think I have) found the source of the problem:

`test_files` (in this case) redefine itself as `test_files_serial` ([test-files.R#L168](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/test-files.R#L168), so some attention could be needed for the parallel version), passing to it the option `test_package = test_package`, which is actually our "`env`" ([auto-test.R#L58](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/auto-test.R#L58)).

From that point, the following chain of functions are called (with the reported arguments):

1. `test_files_setup_state(test_dir, test_package, load_helpers, env)`, [test-files.R#L197](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/test-files.R#L197)
2. `local_test_directory(test_dir, test_package, .env = .env)`, [test-files.R#L229](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/test-files.R#L229) (note also that here the second argument's name is `package`)
3. `local_edition(find_edition(path, package), .env = .env)`, [local.R#L144](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/956fce8672c7b58b6d832e589b5af6b5862cfbf1/R/local.R#L144), and [edition.R#1](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/f1dd05cbae2432c1ad8a3db53849ce01819f4172/R/edition.R#L1)
4. `find_description(path, package)`, [edition.R#L10](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/f1dd05cbae2432c1ad8a3db53849ce01819f4172/R/edition.R#L10)
5. `desc::desc(package = package)`, [edition.R#L12](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/f1dd05cbae2432c1ad8a3db53849ce01819f4172/R/edition.R#L12)

and `desc::desc(package = package)` returned "Error: package is not a string" because `package` is actually our `env`.

title: Helpers are scoped correctly with R CMD check but not `devtools::test()`
description:
This concerns both CRAN and dev testthat. Add these files to a package:

```diff
2 files changed, 5 insertions(+)
tests/testthat/helper-test.R | 1 +
tests/testthat/test-test.R   | 4 ++++

new file   tests/testthat/helper-test.R
@@ -0,0 +1 @@
+list <- list("my list")
new file   tests/testthat/test-test.R
@@ -0,0 +1,4 @@
+
+test_that("helper is in scope", {
+  expect_equal(list, list("my list"))
+})
```

This fails with `devtools::test()`:

```
✔ |  OK F W S | Context
✖ |   0 1     | test [0.1 s]
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Failure (test-test.R:3:3): helper is in scope
`list` (`actual`) not equal to list("my list") (`expected`).

`actual` is a primitive function
`expected` is a list
```

But works fine with R CMD check.

This worked with `test()` in testthat pre-3.0.

title: Nested expect_error(expect_warning(*)) ignores warning message
description:
If you use `expect_warning` on its own, it will detect whether the warning message matches a given value:

```r
expect_warning(warning("here is a warning"), "bad")
# Error: `warning("here is a warning")` produced unexpected warnings.
# Expected match: bad
# Actual values:
# * here is a warning
```

However, if the `expect_warning` is inside an `expect_error` call, the warning message is ignored:

```r
expect_error(
    expect_warning(
        {
            warning("here is a warning")
            stop("here is an error")
        },
        "bad"
    ),
    "error"
)
# (no output)
```

Is this intended? Note that the error message is NOT ignored:

```r
expect_error(
    expect_warning(
        {
            warning("here is a warning")
            stop("here is an error")
        },
        "bad"
    ),
    "bad2"
)
# Error: `expect_warning(...)` threw an error with unexpected message.
# Expected match: "bad2"
# Actual message: "here is an error"
```

This is with testthat 3.0.1 and devtools 2.3.2.

title: expect_s3_class() should handle not-S3 classes [FR]
description:
In some cases, you want to remove a class from an object.

Then, if you removed the last S3 class, you should obviously expect an object without any S3 class.

However, `expect_s3_class()` will not allow testing if an object is no longer an S3 class.

Here is a simple example with labels, using `expss:::unlab.default()`:

``` rmd
library(expss)
library(testthat)
x=iris
class(x$Sepal.Length)
#> [1] "numeric"
var_lab(x$Sepal.Length) = "Sepal length"
var_lab(x$Sepal.Length)
#> [1] "Sepal length"
class(x$Sepal.Length)
#> [1] "labelled" "numeric"
expect_s3_class(x$Sepal.Length, "labelled/numeric")
#> Error: x$Sepal.Length inherits from `labelled/numeric` not `labelled/numeric`.
x$Sepal.Length = unlab(x$Sepal.Length)
class(x$Sepal.Length)
#> [1] "numeric"
expect_s3_class(x$Sepal.Length, "numeric")
#> Error: x$Sepal.Length is not an S3 object
expect_s3_class(x$Sepal.Length, NULL)
#> Error in expect_s3_class(x$Sepal.Length, NULL): is.character(class) is not TRUE
```

<sup>Created on 2021-02-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

Here are some potential syntaxes I could think of:

- `expect_s3_class(x$Sepal.Length, NULL)`
- `expect_s3_class(x$Sepal.Length, isS3=FALSE)`
- `expect_not_s3(x$Sepal.Length)`

IMHO, the first one feels the most logical and should be the easiest to implement.


#### EDIT:

As you can see, I've been confused by the error message "Error: x$Sepal.Length inherits from `labelled/numeric` not `labelled/numeric`.". See https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/1322.

title: Error message in expect_s3_class() is confusing
description:
During testing, it can be common to make some trial-and-error.

This can lead to this kind of awkward error message.

``` r
library(testthat)
x=iris
class(x$Sepal.Length)
#> [1] "numeric"
typeof(x$Sepal.Length)
#> [1] "double"
expss::var_lab(x$Sepal.Length) = "Sepal length"

#lets say I mixed the concepts of classes and types
expect_s3_class(x$Sepal.Length, "double")
#> Error: x$Sepal.Length inherits from `labelled/numeric` not `double`.

expect_s3_class(x$Sepal.Length, "labelled/numeric")
#> Error: x$Sepal.Length inherits from `labelled/numeric` not `labelled/numeric`.
```
<sup>Created on 2021-02-07 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v1.0.0)</sup>

Maybe this function can either accept this syntax or specifically handle this situation (for instance by throwing a special message when a class contains `/`).

title: `expect_match()` documentation
description:
Thanks for another great package! I'm new to {testthat} and am having trouble sorting through the documentation on `expect_match()`. I'd like to make my tests in line with the [3rd edition](https://testthat.r-lib.org/articles/third-edition.html), and I'm unclear as to whether `expect_match()` is being soft-deprecated. It's not listed in the [Reference](https://testthat.r-lib.org/reference/index.html) but I'm not seeing any deprecation flag on the [function documentation](https://testthat.r-lib.org/reference/expect_match.html). I also see it in the latest [R packages](https://r-pkgs.org/tests.html#expectations) but then see the function was [marked as internal](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/commit/6325a41426b5495e68e8d3773dce095e73bfafd9).

In short, should new tests avoid using `expect_match()` and instead use `expect_identical()`, `expect_equal()`, or `expect_true()`?

Thank you!

title: expect_equal should indicate differing names
description:
```r
testthat::test_that("muckity", {
  muckity <- c(A="B",C="D",E="F")
  testthat::expect_equal(muckity, c(A="B",C="D",OOPS="F"))
})
```

Running this snippet gives the output:

title: offer idiom to reuse fixture / setup code in vignettes, examples, docs
description:
I like to reuse the fixture / setup code I use (and test) in testthat across other places in the package, such as vignettes, example, docs.

This might be best explained with an example (pseudocode):

Say, I have a `tests/testthat/test-foo.R`:

```r
test_that("foofy can add two numbers", {
  out <- source(test_path(foofy.R))
  expect_equal(out, 2)
})
```

The setup / example code lives in `tests/testthat/foofy.R`:

```r
foofy(1, 1)
```

I then reuse this in the roxygen2 documentation with the `@example "tests/testthat/foofy.R` tag, as well as in a vignette with a knitr `child = "../tests/testthat/foofy.R` document.
Obviously, the code in `tests/testthat/foofy.R` would be longer; typically for setting up some data structure.

I like this because:

1. It can reduce code duplication somewhat (see this [PR in roxygen](https://github.com/r-lib/roxygen2/pull/1193), for example)
2. It makes it easier to change things.
3. It gets me some way to a [Design-by-Contract (DbC)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Design_by_contract) paradigm, where I make sure that everything I promise the users in the vignette and the examples is actually also tested.
4. It makes me provide more, better tests and examples, because I only have to go through the pain once.

This works fine, and there's not necessarily any technical aspect missing, but the above practice:

1. Deposits information that belongs together in yet more files.
2. There can be quite a lot of `tests/testthat/foofy.R`-type files.
3. The long relative paths can be somewhat disorienting.

In other words: The whole thing isn't very idiomatic, and can easily make life harder for collaborators, because they have *another* thing to figure out.

It would be nice to have some canonical way to do this.

I'm not sure what the answer to this is, or if testthat would even be the right place.

Some preliminary ideas:

- Maybe just extending `test_path()` with a new friend or feature, to also find paths from inside vignettes and pkg root (for roxygen2 `#' @example`).
- Maybe recommend a different directory for where these setup pieces / examples should be stored?

Happy to start a PR on this if there's some interest and guidance.

title: Add skip_if_windows (or skip_if_platform("Windows"))
description:
This would basically be a wrapper:

```
skip_if(.Platform$OS.type == "windows")
```

The benefit is (1) as developer, I tend to forget the exact sequence needed -- is Windows the one that is funny, or is it Mac? Which `.Platform` key was it again? (2) as a reviewer, `skip_if_windows()` is easier to grok.

Mac is also somewhat finnicky to get right (I have to look it up every time), so this would also apply to Mac (perhaps even moreso), but skipping on Mac is more rare, whereas the frequency of skipping on Windows is [cited in the docs](https://testthat.r-lib.org/articles/skipping.html):

> Skipping is a relatively advanced topic because in most cases you want all your tests to run everywhere. The most common exceptions are.. relying on features that not all operating systems possess... This platform tends to be Windows, since amongst other things, it lacks full utf8 support.

Happy to file a PR, just checking it'll be accepted/upfront feedback on API.

title: tests fail with system(wait = FALSE) with R 3.6 on Windows
description:
I have a function in my package that starts an external program using `system("my commands", intern = FALSE, wait = FALSE)`. 

This has been working for a long time, and my tests of this function also work. But recently my tests have started running indefinitely and I have narrowed down the problem to the fact that `testthat` does not seem to be honouring the `wait = FALSE` instruction. This only appears to occur on R 3.6 on Windows, and as the problem has only started recently I assume it is in some way related to the latest version of `testthat`.

I've tried to produce a simpler reproducible example:

```
# Simple function that will make a system call to Windows command line and then do nothing
# If wait = TRUE, function should take about 4 seconds to run
# If wait = FALSE, functon should return immediately
sleep_test <- function(wait){
  r <- system("ping -n 5 127.0.0.1", intern = wait, wait = wait)
  return(TRUE)
}


test_that("Does not wait", {
  t1 <- Sys.time()
  t <- system.time(sleep_test(FALSE))
  t2 <- Sys.time()
  expect_true(t[[3]] < 1)
  expect_true(as.numeric(difftime(t2,t1)) < 1)
})

test_that("Does wait", {
  t1 <- Sys.time()
  t <- system.time(sleep_test(TRUE))
  t2 <- Sys.time()
  expect_true(t[[3]] > 4)
  expect_true(as.numeric(difftime(t2,t1)) > 4)
})

```
These tests run without any problem if I simply run the script. But if I put them into a package structure and use `devtools::check()` or the `Run Tests` button in RStudio then the tests for "Does not wait" will fail.

Intrestingly the test `expect_true(t[[3]] < 1)` passes but the test `expect_true(as.numeric(difftime(t2,t1)) < 1)` fails.

In my actual use case, I end up with the tests running indefinitely because my `system()` call starts a program. The program is waiting for further instructions from R and R is waiting for the program to finish. Thus both wait forever.

title: Can no longer call `test_path()` directly in an R script
description:
Original issue came from yardstick where i have patched this with https://github.com/tidymodels/yardstick/commit/168a3d5b94b6bff40a3dbeeec2053edadf648627

In testthat 3.0.0, when `test_path()` is called in a `helper-*.R` file, but outside of any function, it now fails with:

```r
> devtools::load_all(".")
ℹ Loading testtestpath
Error: Can't find `tests/testthat/` in current directory.
```

I have made a small test package where this issue occurs
https://github.com/DavisVaughan/testtestpath

In [helper-data.R](https://github.com/DavisVaughan/testtestpath/blob/master/tests/testthat/helper-data.R), I try to load some "expensive" data in one time, so that I can call `get_data()` multiple times throughout testing to access a version of the data that has already been loaded into memory. The `test_path()` call here no longer works.

```r
# This doesn't work with testthat 3.0.0
my_data <- readRDS(test_path("data", "data.rds"))

get_data <- function() {
  my_data

  # This does work in testthat 3.0.0
  # readRDS(test_path("data", "data.rds"))
}
```

title: Document the alternative for testing R6 classes
description:
Until v3.0.0, a typical way to test whether an R6 object is of a specific class was with `expect_is()`. 
Today `expect_is` is deprecated and instead of it, three options are advised: `expect_type()`, `expect_s3_class()`, or `expect_s4_class()` 

None of these suggestions is an adequate replacement when testing R6 objects. For example:

```
Cars <- R6::R6Class(classname = "Cars")


# Before v3.0.0
expect_is(Cars, "R6ClassGenerator") # Pass
expect_is(Cars$new(), "Cars") # Pass

# Today
expect_type(Cars, "R6ClassGenerator")
#> Error: `Cars` has type `environment`, not `R6ClassGenerator`.
expect_type(Cars$new(), "Cars")
#> Error: Cars$new() has type `environment`, not `Cars`.

```

While `expect_type` does exactly what it should do, it doesn't substitute `expect_is` 

What is the advice in testing R6 classes?

title: Parallel tests use different language
description:
I have `Config/testthat/parallel: true` in my DESCRIPTION

```r
data_uris <- function(..., mime = '', encoding = 'base64', files) {
	stopifnot(length(list(...)) == 0L)
	vapply(
		files,
		function(f) base64enc::dataURI(mime = mime, encoding = encoding, file = f),
		character(1L))
}

test_that('Extra arguments to data_uris error', {
	expect_error(
		data_uris('one', mime = 'text/html'),
		'length(list(...)) == 0L is not TRUE',
		fixed = TRUE
	)
})
```

When I run it (edit: with german locale set), I get

```
Error (test_utils.r:3:2): Extra arguments to data_uris error
Error: length(list(...)) == 0L ist nicht TRUE
Backtrace:
 1. testthat::expect_error(...)
 7. repr:::f()
 8. repr::data_uris("one", mime = "text/html")
 9. base::stopifnot(length(list(...)) == 0L) R/utils.r:137:8
```

title: `devtools::check` fails after `use_catch()` without (undocumented) fix
description:
I got the somewhat unexpected result after the last update of testthat to 3.0.0 that `R CMD CHECK` failed for my package which uses Catch due to the new test methods for compiled code and the following line in particular:

https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/45a9c705402bd51af29b9d999e587ba789f6203f/R/test-compiled-code.R#L34

While this can be fixed by adding `Suggests: xml2` to the DESCRIPTION file of my own package, this is undocumented and can only be discovered by getting the error or looking up the code directly. I suggest to either document this dependency in `run_cpp_tests` and adding a message to `use_catch` or placing xml2 again in the imports of testthat. As a user of the Catch-feature, the first approach seems a little unnatural to me as I am not using the xml2 package directly and it seems to be more of an implementation detail of testthat, but I understand that xml2 might be an unnecessary dependency for most testthat users.

description:
In testthat v3:
```

+     warning("W1")
+   })
+

+     warning("W3")
+   })
+ })

W3
Backtrace:

 3. testthat:::quasi_capture(...)

```

I did some debugging: 

On the second warning signalled under expect_warning() the condition `!is.null(matched) || !matches(cnd)` in `capture_matching_condition()` (https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/expect-condition.R#L262) evaluates to `TRUE`. Should it read `!is.null(matched) && !matches(cnd)` instead?

title: double negation in skip_if_not() message
description:
The `message` in `skip_if_not()` is always appended with " is not TRUE". This makes sense for the `deparse(substitute(condition))` default. It may not for custom messages. 

Case in point is the googledrive package, where `skip_if_not(drive_has_token(), "No Drive token")` [results in](https://github.com/tidyverse/googledrive/runs/1391398269?check_suite_focus=true#step:11:36) "No Drive token is not TRUE".

This can be easily fixed IMHO if `skip_if_not()` is modelled after `skip_if()`, i.e. if custom messages are shown as is and only the default message is "{condition} is not TRUE".

I can make a PR, if you agree.

title: `remove_source()` doesn't work with nested functions
expect_snapshot_value( style = "serialize") should store data binary, but it converts it to ASCII
description:
https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/efaf620af6823d0658cb16e6a1e1676624a790f6/R/snapshot.R#L127-L151

For me this was an unexpected behavior, as the reference states that it will be saved as a binary object. So is this intended?

And if yes, could there be an option included to choose between ASCII & binary?

Because to quote the R manual:

"ASCII saves used to be useful for moving data between platforms but are now mainly of historical interest. They can be more compact than binary saves where compression is not used, but are almost always slower to both read and write: binary saves compress much better than ASCII ones. Further, decimal ASCII saves may not restore double/complex values exactly, and what value is restored may depend on the R platform. "
https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/save.html

And it is indeed very slow in my case.

title: character context issue
description:
When running tests using **testthat::file** in the __RStudio__ console, tests works fine. Running the same test using shortcut __CTRL + SHIFT + T__, runs the test and it systematically fails. I instrumented the test to get some contextual information to be able to at least identify the most probable issue source. Refer to attached picture. It shows at north east the test file used, at south east the console test run results and at north west the test pane results. Red arrows points the main issue. **Character order in console and in test context does not appear to be the same**. I deal only with ascii compatible characters. See **sessionInfo()** output below for contextual and system information. Not only, I wonder why, but more surely, I guess this is simply wrong. if (basename(getwd()) == "testthat" && basename(dirname(getwd())) == "tests") {

}

title: expect_error() not (always) catched in test_local()
description:
I found a strange testing behaviour when testing package collapse 1.4.2 (I am not the author of that package):
Errors tested for with `expect_error()` are not (always?) catched by `test_local()` but slip through, resulting in a non-successful test result and a crashed R session.

When running `test_local()`, the testing fails and the R session crashes with testthat 3.0:

```
Loading collapse
collapse 1.4.2, see ?`collapse-package` or ?`collapse-documentation`
Note: stats::D  ->  D.expression, D.call, D.name

== Testing test-fbetween-fwithin-B-W.R
=========================================
[ FAIL 0 | WARN 0 | SKIP 0 | PASS 295 ]Not compatible with requested
type: [type=character; target=double].
Exited with status 3.
```
Same happens if I press the "Run Tests" button in R Studio on the specific file.
Sames is true for testthat 2.3.2's `test_package()`.
The error does not occur within `R CMD check`.

(With 3.0, `test_package("collapse")` returns `No installed testthat tests found for collapse`, which I found strange, but seems to be an unrelated issue.)

However, when I test only the specific file with `test_file("./tests/testthat/test-fbetween-fwithin-B-W.R")`, all tests pass.

Here is a reduced reproducible (for me...) example, i.e. how a testthat test file from within the package's source would look like:
```
context("fbetween / B and fwithin / W - reduced")

mtcNA <- na_insert(mtcars)
mtcNA[1,1] <- NA # single group NA !!
m <- as.matrix(mtcars)
mNA <- as.matrix(mtcNA)
mNAc <- mNA
storage.mode(mNAc) <- "character"

test_that("fbetween produces errors for wrong input", {
  expect_error(fbetween("a"))
})
```

title: Testthat errors out with 'no item called "imports" on the search list'
description:
In preparation for a new release of the `import` package (see [here](https://github.com/smbache/import)), I have been adding unit tests through testthat. However, although the tests work when sourced interactively (or through `reprex::reprex()`), they fail when run through `devtools::test()`.

The error message is  `no item called "imports" on the search list` (`imports` is the name of the environment into which the functions are being imported), so I'm guessing that the creation of the environment (search list entry) is failing.

I realize that it is not obvious that a test should be able to create a search list entry in a protected environment such as the testthat tests. And in fact, I've jerry-rigged an alternative test harness that starts up an `Rscript` process to run each of the unit test files. I then use `expect_match()` in the main process to check if the Rscript proces got through the file without any issues. Clunky, but this actually works fine locally (both on MacOS and Windows), but on GitHub Actions (Windows only), that approach fails for strange reasons and this is precluding CI from running the unit tests on Windows.

So, I'm really hoping that there is a setting or other way to do the tests inside the testthat environment, instead starting a new process, because this `Rscript` workaround is probably always going to be quite fragile.

Below is a (hopefully reproducible) demonstration of this issue. 

First a how this works outside `devtools::test()` (this is an actual `reprex::reprex()`, but no output was expected, just that it runs without error):
``` r
library(testthat)
context("Demonstration of search list issue")
test_that("Basic import works", {
  expect_silent( import::from(dplyr, select) )
})
```

Then the results of a running `devtools::test()` with a file containing the above text in the `testthat` directory.

```
==> devtools::test()

Loading import
The import package should not be attached.
Use "colon syntax" instead, e.g. import::from, or import:::from.
Testing import

─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
test_import.R:9: error: Basic import works
no item called "imports" on the search list
Backtrace:

  9. import::from(dplyr, select)

```

title: Dynamically assign variable to object to use both in setup and in unit tests
description:
Dear All,

In our CI pipeline we currently test that an API (built with plumber) can be succesfully run in a sub process and run the tests defined by the developer. We follow the same framework as in plumbpkg: https://github.com/sol-eng/plumbpkg/blob/master/tests/testthat/test-plumber.R 

My question is how can we set the port dynamically? One needs first to make sure that the port on the server running the CI tests is available and then use the same value in the tests. How can this be achieved? Here below is an example of tests that succeed if the port variable is explicitely written, but the following code where `port` is defined as a global variable fails:

```
port <<- 1879 # or a function that finds an available port
alive_url <<- glue::glue("http://localhost:{port}/alive")

testthat::setup({
  process <<- callr::r_bg(
    function() {
      r <- plumber::plumb(file = system.file("plumber", "api1", "plumber.R", package = "mycustom.api"))
      r$run(host = "0.0.0.0", port = port, swagger = FALSE)
    }
  )
})

Sys.sleep(5)

testthat::teardown({
  process$kill()
})

testthat::test_that("Process is alive", {
  testthat::expect_true(process$is_alive())
})

test_that("alive_url returns 200", {
  r <- httr::GET(alive_url)
  expect_equal(r$status_code, 200)
})
```

Output here:
```
── 1. Failure: Process is alive (@test-plumber.R#32)  ────────────────────
process$is_alive() isn't true.

── 2. Error: alive_url returns 200 (@test-plumber.R#38)  ─────────────────
Failed connect to localhost:1879; Connection refused
Backtrace:
 1. httr::GET(alive_url)
 2. httr:::request_perform(req, hu$handle$handle)
 4. httr:::request_fetch.write_memory(req$output, req$url, handle)
 5. curl::curl_fetch_memory(url, handle = handle)

══ testthat results  ═════════════════════════════════════════════════════
[ OK: 1 | SKIPPED: 0 | WARNINGS: 0 | FAILED: 2 ]
1. Failure: Process is alive (@test-plumber.R#32) 
2. Error: alive_url returns 200 (@test-plumber.R#38) 
```

There might be something I misunderstand about `testthat::setup` as it seems that global variable set outside it are not accessible. Can anyone help with this issue?

Best regards,
Alessandro

title: Test case failure on older R versions because `options(warnPartialMatchArgs = NULL)` fails
description:
Before R 3.6.0 
```
options(warnPartialMatchArgs = NULL)
```
errors, and now withr does not ignore failures in deferred code, so we get an error when we use 
```
  withr::local_options(list(warnPartialMatchArgs = FALSE))
```
in a test case. 

I'll submit a PR with a workaround in a minute.

title: Feature request: test_examples() with run.dontrun and run.donttest
description:
Thanks for this package!

I expected the `test_example()` and `test_examples()` functions to have parameters `run.dontrun` and `run.donttest`, just like `utils::example()`.

I agree with what you say in the man page (`?test_examples`):

> Generally, this is redundant with R CMD check, and is not recommended in routine practice.

But as the CRAN maintainers have requested us to decrease the time it takes to run the (nonetheless vey useful) examples, we put some of them in `\donttest{}`. Would be great if we could run them in our `testthat` routine with every git commit.

Or parameters like `only_dontrun` and `only_donttest` would also be tremendously useful IMHO. Could be this be considered?

title: R6 classes with mocked functions support
Faster parallel startup
description:
Parallel startup is really slow currently. It includes
* starting the R process
* loading testthat
* loading the tested package + helpers
* running setup files

For 4 processes this takes ~ 2.5 seconds for testthat. For a better interactive performance we could keep the sub-processes alive if the session is interactive.

title: Loaded functions overriding helper-data variables with same name
description:
If a variable in the helper-data.R file has the same name as a loaded function, the function is used instead of the variable while running tests. For a simple repro, create the following two files in a testthat directory:

_helper-data.R_
```
abs = 1:5
something_else = 5:1
```

_test-repro.R_
```
str(abs)
str(something_else)
```

_output from devtools::test()_
```
function (x)  
 int [1:5] 5 4 3 2 1
```

This issue only started happening when I built a new computer and installed R version 4. Currently have the latest version of testthat installed (2.4.2). On my old computer with R 3.6, it was not an issue, but I also probably had an older version of testthat installed, so I don't know if the change in behavior originated with R or the testthat package.

title: Cannot library(tidyr) when using testthat::test_file
description:
Inside a [function](https://github.com/tbrown122387/gradeR/blob/47a6efdcd7e73779606c13ee17b78a8adb32a74e/R/grade.r#L192) I am 

- creating a new environment (call it `testEnv`),
- `source`ing some script (call it `code.R`) and storing the results in this new environment, and
- calling `testthat::test_file` with the argument `env = new.env(parent = testEnv))` to evaluate some tests found in a file (call it `test_file.R`).

This has always worked just fine. But the problems started once I attach `tidyr` inside `code.R`, or in other words, when I insert the line 

```
library(tidyr)
```

into `code.R`. When I add this one line, all the tests that used to be pass now fail. When I ssh into the server, when I am running `R` interactively, I can `library(tidyr)` just fine. So I think that the script is being sourced just fine, and it's `test_file` that's not able to find the variables that were sourced in.

My questions are:

1. why is this happening,
2. even though I think I am running the tests **after** I source `code.R`, could calling `library(tidyr)` in `code.R` cause `testthat::matches` to be masked by masked by `tidyr::matches` to be masked, and
3. if so, why would that matter, and 
4. does this have anything to do with the following sentence found in the documentation to `test_file`: "[y]ou are responsible for ensuring that the functions to test are available in the global environment."
 
I have tried removing `library(testthat)` from `test_file.R`, and instead prefixing all the function calls with `testthat::` but the same problem occurs.

title: allow callers to 'detect' skips without requiring reporter
description:
Right now, skips are caught and swallowed within a `tryCatch()` handler:

https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/9e643d8ee9772c58d5a6bf0846e16bf78dde59f9/R/test-that.R#L193-L194

However, it'd be useful if that condition could be re-signaled for other entities (other than reporters) which might want to react to that signal. That is, I'd like for the following to work:

```
library(testthat)

skipped <- FALSE
withCallingHandlers(
  test_that("skips can be handled", skip("skip")),
  skip = function(e) skipped <<- TRUE
)

identical(skipped, TRUE)
```

title: should crayon be enabled in 2nd edition?
description:
The new stuff looks great!

I found one place in my package where the backwards compatibility falls down - in the CRAN version of testthat, crayon printing is enabled, but in the dev even in "2nd edition mode" it is not.

In the CRAN version, both of these tests work, but in dev the first fails. The work around in the second seems reasonable, but figured I'd mention in light of the focus on backwards compatibility.

``` r
library(testthat)

hello <- function() {
    crayon::bgWhite("Hello, world!")
}

test_that("crayon turned off in testthat dev version", {
    expect_equal(hello(), "\033[47mHello, world!\033[49m")
})
#> ── <text>:8:5: failure: crayon turned off in testthat dev version ─────────────────
#> hello() not equal to "\033[47mHello, world!\033[49m".
#> 1/1 mismatches
#> x[1]: "Hello, world!"
#> y[1]: "\033[47mHello, world!\033[49m"

test_that("an okay fix", {
    options(crayon.enabled = TRUE)
    expect_equal(hello(), "\033[47mHello, world!\033[49m")
})
#> Test passed 🥇
```

test_that("new_observations() checks that endDate + 1 is in history", {

  dfhist <- data.frame(dates=as.Date('2019-11-01'), values=100)

})

title: Confirm local_edition() is fully functional
description:
In my hands, `local_edition()` doesn't seem to work as widely as promised (emphasis mine):

>` local_edition()` allows you to temporarily (within a single test or a **single test file**) change the active edition of testthat.

Specifically, I only get its effect *inside* a test.

I don't know how to reconcile what I'm seeing with what I see in this vignette: https://testthat.r-lib.org/articles/third-edition.html, where `local_edition()` *appears* to have the documented scope. But maybe some global option is also in effect when that vignette is rendered.

``` r
library(testthat)

packageVersion("testthat")
#> [1] '2.99.0.9000'

# something's definitely happening!
local_edition(3)
#> Setting deferred event(s) on global environment.
#>   * Execute (and clear) with `deferred_run()`.
#>   * Clear (without executing) with `deferred_clear()`.

# I'm still getting "old" testthat behaviour, i.e. no waldo
expect_equal(structure("good", class = "foofy"), "good")
#> Error: structure("good", class = "foofy") not equal to "good".
#> Attributes: < Modes: list, NULL >
#> Attributes: < Lengths: 1, 0 >
#> Attributes: < names for target but not for current >
#> Attributes: < current is not list-like >
#> target is foofy, current is character

# I'm still getting "old" testthat behaviour, i.e. no waldo
test_that("I understand how to wield local_edition()", {
  expect_equal(structure("good", class = "foofy"), "good")  
})
#> ── <text>:13:3: failure: I understand how to wield local_edition() ───────────────────
#> structure("good", class = "foofy") not equal to "good".
#> Attributes: < Modes: list, NULL >
#> Attributes: < Lengths: 1, 0 >
#> Attributes: < names for target but not for current >
#> Attributes: < current is not list-like >
#> target is foofy, current is character

# NOW I get 3e behaviour, i.e. waldo comparison
test_that("I understand how to wield local_edition()", {
  local_edition(3)
  expect_equal(structure("good", class = "foofy"), "good")  
})
#> ── <text>:19:3: failure: I understand how to wield local_edition() ───────────────────
#> structure("good", class = "foofy") (`actual`) not equal to "good" (`expected`).
#> 
#> `actual` is an S3 object of class <foofy>
#> `expected` is a character vector ('good')
```

title: `expect_snapshot_value()` and functions/environments doesn't work well
description:
It seems that `expect_snapshot_value()` cannot be used when functions/environments are involved. Is there any chance to make this work or a good workaround?

I wasn't able to directly produce an example with `reprex()`. Copy the following in a file and run it with `test_file()` to see the issues

```r
test_that("json", {
  expect_snapshot_value(
    function(x) x,
    style = "json"
  )
})

test_that("json2", {
  expect_snapshot_value(
    function(x) x,
    style = "json2"
  )
})

test_that("deparse", {
  expect_snapshot_value(
    function(x) x,
    style = "deparse"
  )
})

test_that("serialize", {
  expect_snapshot_value(
    function(x) x,
    style = "serialize"
  )
})
```

and the results

```
── test-blub.R:2:3: error: json ───────────────────────────────────────────
Error: Serialization round-trip is not symmetric.

`value` is a function
`roundtrip` is a list

i You may need to consider serialization `style`
Backtrace:
 1. testthat::expect_snapshot_value(function(x) x, style = "json") test-blub.R:2:2
 2. testthat:::expect_snapshot_helper(...)
 3. snapshotter$take_snapshot(val, save = save, load = load)
 4. testthat:::check_roundtrip(value, load(save(value)))

── test-blub.R:1:1: warning: (code run outside of `test_that()`) ──────────
Snapshots reset after error/skip

── test-blub.R:9:3: error: json2 ──────────────────────────────────────────
Error: Serialization round-trip is not symmetric.

`attr(environment(value), 'handlers')` is absent

about this code:

set.seed(2020)

b) Create a .RData file containing the matrix and then load it in `test-foo.R`

Tanks in advance!
Noelia

title: Consider adding a replacement for expect_known_hash() in 3e
description:
In the NEWS for testthat 3e, you mention:

> expect_known_output(), expect_known_value(), expect_known_hash(), and expect_equal_to_reference() are all deprecated in favour of expect_snapshot_output() and expect_snapshot_value()

But I think one important use case is not covered by expect_snapshot_value().

I use hashes because they are a very space-efficient representation of possibly very large objects. I have several dozens of tests for functions that produce relatively large objects. If I were to use `expect_snapshot_value()`, I would very quickly go over the 5 MB limit on CRAN. I also don't think adding these files to `.Rbuildignore` would be a satisfactory solution as I want these tests to run on CRAN (with `cran = TRUE`).

A possible solution within the framework you defined for 3e would be to add `style = "hash"` as an option in `expect_snapshot_value()` and it would save the hash in the snapshot file.

title: expect_snapshot()
description:
Implement new snapshot mechanism inspired by jest and discussions with @jcheng5 (much in #1017)

```R
# in test-foo.R
test_that("title", {
  expect_snapshot(complicated())
})
```

On first run, would create `tests/testthat/snapshots/foo.yaml` containing:

```yaml
title:
- output of complicated()
```

On subsequent runs, would generate `tests/testthat/snapshots/foo.yaml.new`. If no difference from the previous run, the test succeeds and the file is be automatically deleted. If there are differences, the test fails. If it's a deliberate change, you run `snapshot_update()` to update stored snapshots.

At the end of the complete test run, all obsolete snapshots are automatically deleted.

When `expect_snapshot()` is run interactively (i.e. no `TESTTHAT_FILE` env var set), it would just print the value.

So we only show the number passing tests, and the rest is shown below. * making the summary line at the end a single line, to save space * showing a nice (full) stack for errors, potentially with references to the source code * showing the nicely highlighted code where the error happened

Creating local functions in testthat files

(if I simply copy paste the function and corresponding test in the console and run it, it runs without an error or test passes)

For instance, I create a function for selection sort inside the scope of the second parameter for a `test_that` call, which results in a test fail: 
![1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/30123691/87001973-561b1900-c1d6-11ea-9f2b-5f1e3789ab15.png)

Also fails if I put my function outside the test_that block:

There isn't any problem with my function, as I've checked it locally as mentioned:

The other tests all work fine, which include functions from my package, other packages (imports or in suggests), and also normal ones such as the `sort()` function for instance in the pictures above. title: [feature request] more intuitive methods for comparing relative and absolute errors between floating point vectors
description:
I have seen even the most seasoned R users wrongly assuming `expect_equal(float1, float2, tolerance = tol)` would check the absolute error between the actual and expected values, and would only find out that's not the case by first reading `?expect_equal` to realize it uses `all.equal`, and then reading `?all.equal` to see

```
     Numerical comparisons for ‘scale = NULL’ (the default) are
     typically on _relative difference_ scale unless the target values
     are close to zero: First, the mean absolute difference of the two
     numerical vectors is computed.  If this is smaller than
     ‘tolerance’ or not finite, absolute differences are used,
     otherwise relative differences scaled by the mean absolute
     ‘target’ value.  Note that these comparisons are computed only for
     those vector elements where ‘target’ is not ‘NA’ and differs from
     ‘current’.  If ‘countEQ’ is true, the equal and ‘NA’ cases are
     _counted_ in determining “sample” size.
```

and then finally realizing `expect_equal(float1, float2, tolerance = tol, scale = 1)` would actually check for absolute error, whereas what `expect_equal(float1, float2, tolerance = tol)` does is the outcome of some kind of decision tree as vaguely described in `?all.equal`.

This looks to me like too many indirections and cognitive overhead for something simple. It's also error-prone especially for people not reading documentation that well. Why not just have specialized methods `expect_approx_equal(x, y, max_abs_err = <abs tol>)` and `expect_approx_equal(x, y, max_rel_err = <rel tol>)` instead?

title: testthat 3e
description:
There are a number of components of the testthat API that we now regret, but are effectively impossible to remove because 100s of CRAN packages use them, including many packages that are not regularly maintained. Thanks to @jcheng5 I now have a framework for how we might start to more actively re-shape the API for active developers, while leaving the vast majority of packages as is. The key idea is to allow developers to opt-in to an "edition" or version of testthat, using something like  `tests/testthat.yml`, `edition: 2020`.

For this edition, I propose:

* Switching from `all.equal()`/`identical()` to waldo in `expect_equal()` and friends
* Changing the test working directory to the package root, and consequently deprecating `test_path()` (or `setwd(tempdir())` and **require** `test_path()`)
* Running each test file in its own process
* Formally deprecating the old testthat interface based around `expect_that()`
* Formally deprecating `context()` — needs some work to remove internal usage prior to deprecation.
* Formally deprecating bare expectations, `expect_is()`, `compare()`, `expect_known_output()`, ...
* Making `takes_less_than()`, `not()`, `expect_less_than()`, and `expect_greater_than()` defunct
* Deprecate `setup()` and `teardown()` in favour of test fixtures.
* `inst/testthat` should error

As a carrot for upgrading, we'd also make parallel tests available only for this edition.

title: Feedback on verify_output
description:
## Feedback on verify_output

First, I have to say that even with the following obstacles, this was SO much better than not having snapshot-based testing. I was able to pull out dozens of lines of tedious and fragile rote test code and replace with a single `snapshot(obj)` (that's what I called my [helper function](https://github.com/rich-iannone/blastula/blob/c2b618fd8120ece8efb0e8905dbe870b66b8e657/tests/testthat/helpers-snapshot.R)), over and over.

That said, here are the things I noticed after a couple of hours of use.

1. **The automatically-overwriting-the-snapshot behavior feels like a bad tradeoff to me.** Say the golden snapshot is correct and your new code has introduced a bug that the snapshot test has caught. You'd want to be able to keep changing your code and rerunning the tests until the snapshots pass. Instead, after each failed run, the incorrect snapshot has now become the golden. You have to remember to git revert before each subsequent run. More dangerously, say you _are_ expecting the snapshot to change, as you iteratively modify your code. Once you get to a good-but-intermediate state, you have to be careful to stage the changes in your working copy into your git index, otherwise it'll be very easy to overlook when you've diverged from that intermediate state!
2. **The need to manually specify a path for the snapshot felt tedious**; I wrote a helper function but convention over configuration would be my preference. Furthermore, if testthat had a known directory dedicated for each test context, after each (passing) run it could identify snapshots that are obsolete. (Jest does this automatically, it's very nice.) As it is, before checking in I have to blow away the snapshot directory and run the tests one more time.
3. Following on the previous two points, I'd like to see a workflow where **_adding new_ and *removing obsolete* snapshots can be done automatically with just a warning, but *updating existing* snapshots requires a low-friction but deliberate user interaction**. Jest has a watch mode that makes this ridiculously easy, you just press the letter "u" in the terminal and all changed snapshots are updated; or "i" and you get to approve snapshots one by one. [See demo](https://jestjs.io/docs/en/snapshot-testing#interactive-snapshot-mode)
4. **The automatic `print()` didn't work well for my use case,** where the thing I'm trying to snapshot normally displays itself in a browser. (It was a blastula email but could equally have been any htmlwidget.) And long strings with embedded newlines didn't diff well, since everything ends up smooshed into one string element; I used `cat()` instead. It's possible my scenario is just different than what `verify_output` was intended for; I'm sure `verify_output` works great for ensuring that your console print behavior is as desired, while I'm trying to ensure the data itself is consistent even if it's weirdly shaped.
5. **On Windows, emitting a string containing "\r\n" would result in a snapshot that would never verify.** I think the in-memory version contains "\r\n", but when the snapshot is read from disk, it's normalized to "\n"? Something like that. In my case, the fact that the string contains "\r\n" and not "\n" is crucial, so I had to resort to [this](https://github.com/rich-iannone/blastula/blob/c2b618fd8120ece8efb0e8905dbe870b66b8e657/tests/testthat/test-integration.R#L77-L85). I'd be happy to come up with a minimal reprex if needed.
6. I don't have a suggestion for how to fix this, but **dealing with nondeterministic output was challenging;** in my case, I was snapshotting MIME-encoded emails, which contain a Date header at the top and UUID-based boundary markers. Fortunately in my case it was straightforward to use a hardcoded date in my test, and add a level of indirection to the UUID-generation logic so I could use deterministic values. If I had not been able to do that, I would've wanted to maybe post-process the snapshot output to gsub out the problematic areas.

Thanks for this feature, I'll be using it regardless!

title: Make it easier to develop tests when crayon is in use
description:
This happens a lot when I'm developing tests that inspect a crayon-style message:

```
> test_that("check_uses_github_actions() can throw error", {
+   create_local_package()
+   expect_error(
+     check_uses_github_actions(),
+     "Do you need to run `use_github_actions()`?",
+     fixed = TRUE, class = "usethis_error"
+   )
+ })
Error: Test failed: 'check_uses_github_actions() can throw error'
* `check_uses_github_actions()` threw an error with unexpected message.
Expected match: "Do you need to run `use_github_actions()`?"
Actual message: "Cannot detect that package \033[34m'testpkg900b3aef5ec1'\033[39m already uses GitHub Actions.\nDo you need to run \033[90m`use_github_actions()`\033[39m?"
Backtrace:
 1. testthat::expect_error(...)
 6. usethis::check_uses_github_actions()
 7. usethis::ui_stop("\n    Cannot detect that package {ui_value(project_name(base_path))} already \\\n    uses GitHub Actions.\n    Do you need to run {ui_code('use_github_actions()')}?\n    ") UsersjennyrrrusethisRgithub-actions.R:55:2
Backtrace:
    █
 1. └─testthat::test_that(...)
 2.   └─testthat:::test_code(desc, code, env = parent.frame())
 3.     └─get_reporter()$end_test(context = get_reporter()$.context, test = test)
```

In "production", this won't be a problem because the option `crayon.enabled` will be `FALSE` and the message won't contain the escapes.

Yes, I can always set `options("crayon.enabled" = FALSE)` in the session I'm working in, but then I lose lots of *nice* uses of crayon.

Is there any reason to not strip ANSI escapes from all messages inspected in functions like `expect_error()`?

title: The `context_name()` function also removes internal `[.][rR]`; should only be terminal pattern
description:
Currently when creating the name for testing contexts, `context_name()` removes *all* instances of "`\\.[Rr]`" in the name, not only the terminal one. If following convention to match the `test-*.R` filename with the function name it tests may sometimes require a `.R` to exist internally. For example:

`test-calculate.RobustMetrics.R`

```
reprex::reprex({
  library(testthat)
  writeLines(
    "test_that('multiplication works', { expect_equal(2 * 2, 4) })",
    "test-calculate.RobustMetrics.R"
  )
  
  # Context below has '.R' removed from file name
  # Resulting in `calculateobustMetrics`
  test_file("test-calculate.RobustMetrics.R")   
})
```

This of course doesn't usually happen using `tidyverse` function naming conventions, but some organizations may have differing style guides preventing this adherence. 

Suggest a more strict regular expression within `context_name()`, for example:

```
context_name <- function (filename) {
    filename <- gsub("^test-", "", filename)      # add regex starts-with '^'; could use `sub()` instead
    filename <- gsub("[.][Rr]$", "", filename)    # add regex ends-with '$'; could use `sub()` instead
    filename
}
```

As mentioned above, one could also use `sub()` rather than `gsub()`, since we're only interested in the starting (`^`) and terminal (`$`) pattern.
