title: Issues with %in% tests
description:
Hello,

I have realised that `testthat` tests fail on r oldrel specifically for `%in%` due to error messages not matching the actual error. An example from a [package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_mde.html) I maintain:

>Expected match: "sort_by should be a valid name in the output of na_summary"
     Actual message: "sort_by %in% names(res) is not TRUE"

This is also a problem in another [package](https://cran.r-project.org/web/checks/check_results_manymodelr.html):

>   Expected match: "Only forward and reverse are supported"
     Actual message: "direction %in% c(\"forward\", \"reverse\") is not TRUE"

I've looked at using [skip_on_oldrel](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/571) (I don't remember the exact name of the function) but not sure how to use this or if this is what it is actually intended to do.

Thank you.

title: verify_output fails on Linux if there is no X11
description:
In general it fails if there is on png() device.

TBH I am not sure if it is testthat's business to deal with graphic output at all, but at this point we might not be able to change this.

We could still use a more minimal device, e.g. the devoid package could be handy here?

title: expect_inform()
description:
Motivated by me transitioning packages to communicate with the user via `rlang::inform()`.

Since `inform()` can potentially send output to stdout or stderr, depending on the context, I think it would be nice to have an `expect_inform()` that just does the right thing, so you never have to remember whether it should be `expect_message()` or `expect_output()`.

This also means that if `inform()` ever changed again (not super likely, I realize) and `expect_inform()` was duly updated, lots of tests and packages would just continue to work. Most of the usethis v1.6.0 revdep issues were around people testing our output. Now, that's already a red flag, for sure, but the stdout vs stderr thing also came up.

title: Reconsider directory layout
description:
(i.e. the working directory needs to be the project root)

This needs to be a long term plan, but would make testthat more consistent with other packages. Would need to start by emitting warnings so that R CMD check doesn't fail, but you're encouraged to update your tests.

title: Add support for file-scoped test fixtures
description: To replace `setup()` and `teardown()` functions.  Would probably need to build around `defer()`, adding some new file level handler that testthat would be in charge of initialising and destroying.

title: Make waldo failures into warnings?
description: If `all.equal()` is true, only display waldo issues as warnings?

title: Mention expect_vector() in documentation for expect_length()
description:
The documentation for `expect_length()` says that it checks if a vector has the specified length. But {vctrs} has formalized the concept of a vector's "size", which is often the desired property (rather than its length). The vector size can be tested using `expect_vector()`.

I think it might be helpful to reference `expect_vector()` from the documentation of `expect_length()`, to improve the discoverability of this alternative function. It is needed when using S3 vectors derived from {vctrs} classes.

title: Adding methods to compare() for Bioconductor classes
description:
I write packages that depend heavily on Bioconductor packages and need succinct and descriptive comparisons of those objects when tests fail.  I have created a package to add these comparisons:
https://gitlab.com/coregenomics/testthatbioc/-/blob/master/R/granges.R

Should I open a pull request for adding in `compare.MyClass()` and `format.mismatch_MyClass()` objects?  I'm worried about the dependency bloat it would add to testthat.

Additional problems with my having a separate package to extend `compare` and `format` generics are:

1. I have to use several unexported testthat functions in my implementation linked above which tells me I'm doing something I should not be.
2. Note that my package at the minute has a bug with making those methods visible, because simply modifying my `./tests/testthat.R` to import my `testthatbioc` instead of `testthat` and adding a test still invokes the `compare.default()` method:

```R
test_that("testthatbioc gives expected output", {
    expect_equal(GRanges(c("chr1:100:+",
                           "chr1:200:+",
                           "chr1:150:-",
                           "chr1:250:-")),
                 GRanges(c("chr1:100:+",
                           "chr1:200:+",
                           "chr1:450:-")))
})
```

title: Feature suggestion: redefine equal and identical for tibble
description:
test_equal works differently for comparing two tibbles between version 2 and 3.

I found a number of unit tests I had written failed where they previously passed.

I wonder whether test_equal and test_identical could be defined differently for tibbles.

test_equal could work as pre-vctrs: that the same columns are present and each column has the same data content.

test_identical could work as current tibble 3 test_equal - so structure would be more strictly enforced:

For example, column order would need to be identical.

An interesting gotcha I found is that if you use stats::quantile then the vector is named by default: in tibble 3 the names are preserved to the column - and again if you don’t reproduce the named vector in your unit tests even though in routine data work you probably wouldn’t have considered that important. Likewise preserving or removing groupings, or other attributes.

title: Add a reporter that shows context and individual descriptions
description:
Currently, there is:

1. minimal reporter: shows only green dots
2. summary reporter: shows the context, followed by each context tests as green dots.
3. location reporter: does not show the context, shows the test the description and each individual assertions location

1 and 2 are very minimal and don't print the test_that description. 3 is too verbose. I tried various reporters and I could not find one that shows something like

```
context 1:
description of test 1: ....
description of test 2: ...F.
context 2:
description of test 1: .S...F...

```
Or

```
context 1/description of test 1: .....
context 1/description of test 2: .....
```

In other words, something intermediate between 2 and 3.

```
# Error: 1.02 not equal to 1.0200001.

# [1] 1.02 - 1.02 == -1e-07
```

This output would be most useful if `x` and `y` are totally different; would it make more sense to display the values more exactly if the difference is smaller than `1e-2`?

title: testthat messes up sorting when dealing with different case types
description:
- The minimum reprex needed to demonstrate this bug is a simple package, which can be found [here](https://github.com/sumedh10/test)
- The bug can _only_ be reproduced when running `Cmd + Shift + T` or `devtools::test()`, not by running the individual test file 
- In fact, things work as expected when run in the console _and_ as an individual test file  
- Finally, I was able to reproduce this bug _only_ when dealing with _lower case vs upper case_ letters

This is how `base::sort()` works in R: 

```r
> sort(c("B", "b"))
[1] "b" "B"
```

Similarly, 

```r
> library(dplyr)
> df <- data.frame(test_col = c("B", "b"), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
> print(df)
  test_col
1        B
2        b
> print(arrange(df, test_col))
  test_col
1        b
2        B
```

**tl;dr**

All this is to say that lower case `"b"` is supposed to be _less than_ upper case `"B"`. 

However, in the context of `tests/testthat/test-*`, `base::sort()` and `dplyr::arrange()` don't seem to work as expected (FWIW, `base::order()` and `>` don't seem to work too). However, `stringr::str_sort()` does seem to work fine. 

### Steps to Reproduce 

1. Clone the [repository](https://github.com/sumedh10/test) 
2. Run the tests in `tests/testthat/test-hello.R` either using `Cmd + Shift + T` or `devtools::test()` (not as an individual test file) 
3. You'll notice that two tests fail (only the test for `stringr::str_sort()` passes) -- that's because both `sort()` and `arrange()` don't sort the vector and column as expected

> NOTE: The closest somewhat related comment I was able to dig up is [this](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/341#issuecomment-171324520), though not sure if it relates to the current issue.

title: expect_condition() fails when multiple conditions emitted
description:
This might be my misunderstanding of how `expect_condition()` should work, but...

``` r
library(testthat)

signal <- function(class) {
  condition <- simpleCondition(NULL)
  class(condition) <- c(class, "condition")
  signalCondition(condition)
}

test_that("conditions can be expected", {
  expect_condition(signal("hello"), class = "hello")                     # OK
  expect_condition({signal("hello"); signal("world")}, class = "hello")  # OK
  expect_condition({signal("hello"); signal("world")}, class = "world")  # FAIL
})
#> Error: Test failed: 'conditions can be expected'
#> * <text>:13: `{ ... }` threw an condition with unexpected class.
#> 
#> Backtrace:
#>  1. testthat::expect_condition(...)
```

**On 2.2.0**: 
`remotes::install_version("testthat", "2.2.0")`
``` r
library(rJava)
library(testthat)
.jinit()
.jnew("hello/world", check = TRUE)

expect_error(.jnew("hello/world", check = TRUE))
```
<sup>Created on 2019-11-08 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

**On 2.3.0**: 
`remotes::install_version("testthat", "2.3.0")`
``` r
library(rJava)
library(testthat)
.jinit()
.jnew("hello/world", check = TRUE)
#> Error in .jnew("hello/world", check = TRUE): java.lang.ClassNotFoundException

expect_error(.jnew("hello/world", check = TRUE))
#> Error in ._jobjRef_dollar(x[["jobj"]], name): no field, method or inner class called 'trace'
```

title: Remind users about `expect_error()` for custom conditions if `class` is NULL

Folks are still adjusting to [this warning](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/feb5c939829fb392727ec1511d9d686fef72efe4/R/expect-output.R#L136-L139):

``` r
library(testthat)
custom_condition <- function(message) {
  structure(
    list(message = message),
    class = c("custom", "error", "condition")
  )
}
expect_error(stop(custom_condition("my message")), regexp = "my message")
#> Warning: `stop(custom_condition("my message"))` generated a condition with class custom/error/condition.

```

<sup>Created on 2019-08-02 by the [reprex package](https://reprex.tidyverse.org) (v0.3.0)</sup>

When I first saw it, I did not know it was talking about the `class` argument of `expect_error()`. Just today, I saw similar confusion in the R/stats chatter.

Related: #861 

By the way, thank you for creating and maintaining `testthat`. When I learned about `testthat` 3 years ago, it was my first exposure to unit testing and test-driven development, concepts I still find liberating and foundational.


title: Update global environement with test_check and test_file
description:
I have tests where I mock shiny functions that may be imported and global, the problem was that my mock install function was not working when used inside test_file, here is code that works in test_file:
```R
#' Helper function to be used in test files that overwrite shiny functions (after test
#' you should run clearMocks since they are global and if you run shiny application
#' after test that use mocks it will break)
#'
#' @export
useMocks <- function() {
  observeEvent <- battery::observeEventMock
  assignInNamespace('observeEvent', observeEvent, 'battery')
  assignInNamespace('observeEvent', observeEvent, 'shiny')
  isolate <- battery::isolate
  assignInNamespace('isolate', isolate, 'shiny')
  makeReactiveBinding <- battery::makeReactiveBinding
  assignInNamespace('makeReactiveBinding', makeReactiveBinding, 'shiny')
  renderUI <- battery::renderUI
  assignInNamespace('renderUI', renderUI, 'shiny')
  ## we modify global environment so it update env when function is called not the package
  env <- globalenv()
  env$observeEvent <- observeEvent
  env$isolate <- isolate
  env$renderUI <- renderUI
  env$makeReactiveBinding <- makeReactiveBinding
}
```

Previous version was using `parent.env()` (that didn't work with test_file) above works in `testthat::test_file` and when using `devtools::test()` but with `devtools::check()` that call `test_check("battery")` it fails.

I use code like this because (as in comment) it was not working when testing code in the package.

title: question on stop_on_failure default
description:
I see the following in `?testthat::test_dir`

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/7608904/62001805-19860880-b0be-11e9-8312-3eebdf337a72.png)

Why is the default for `stop_on_failure` in `test_dir()` `FALSE` when it is `TRUE` for `test_package()` and `test_check()`? Is that intentional or an oversight?

In my opinion, the default behavior of a testing framework should be to fail (cause a non-zero exit code) if any tests fail. If you agree with me and this is an oversight, please let me know and I'd be happy to make a PR to change it.

Thanks!

title: expect_same_behavior to expect exactly the same output/error/warning/messages for 2 expressions
description:
In order to build unit tests to check if 2 syntaxes are consistent, I found myself needing a *testthat* function that would allow me to check if two expressions trigger the same output, INCLUDING errors / messages / warnings.

I wrote my own, though I'm sure you'd write it differently. Wouldn't it be a cool addition to the package ? See examples at the bottom.

```
expect_same_behavior <- function(object, expected, ...){
  object_chr <- deparse(substitute(object))
  expected_chr <- deparse(substitute(expected))
  quiet <- purrr::safely(purrr::quietly(identity))
  object   <- eval(substitute(quiet(object)))
  expected <- eval(substitute(quiet(expected)))
  testthat::expect(
    identical(object$result$result, expected$result$result, ...),
    sprintf("`%s` and `%s` don't return the same result.", object_chr, expected_chr))
  testthat::expect(
    identical(object$result$output, expected$result$output, ...),
    sprintf("`%s` and `%s` don't print the same output", object_chr, expected_chr))
  testthat::expect(
    identical(object$result$messages, expected$result$messages, ...),
    sprintf("`%s` and `%s` don't print the same messages", object_chr, expected_chr))
  testthat::expect(
    identical(object$result$warnings, expected$result$warnings, ...),
    sprintf("`%s` and `%s` don't trigger the same warnings", object_chr, expected_chr))
  testthat::expect(
    identical(object$error$message, expected$error$message, ...),
    sprintf("`%s` and `%s` don't trigger the same error", object_chr, expected_chr))
  invisible(NULL)
}

expect_same_behavior(1, 1)
expect_same_behavior(print(1),print(1))
expect_same_behavior(message(1),message(1))
expect_same_behavior(stop(1), stop(1))

expect_same_behavior(1, 2)
#> Error: `1` and `2` don't return the same result.
expect_same_behavior(print(1),1)
#> Error: `print(1)` and `1` don't print the same output
expect_same_behavior(message(1),message(2))
#> Error: `message(1)` and `message(2)` don't print the same messages
expect_same_behavior(stop(1), stop(2))
#> Error: `stop(1)` and `stop(2)` don't trigger the same error
```

title: expect_output / capture_output is broken on non UTF-8 platforms
description:
The problem is that even if the output is not UTF-8, `read_lines` always marks it as UTF-8. Actually, even if you try to output (`cat`) proper UTF-8 like I do below, R will convert it to the native encoding (as much as possible), so the recorded output will not be UTF-8.

The behavior is better on the current stable version (1.0.2), because there readLines is used to read back the output, without a specified encoding, so the encoding of the output will be "unknown". This is still better than the current non-UTF-8 output marked as UTF-8. It also works fine in the checks, even if the encoding is not specified.

This is old testthat (example not self-contained, sorry):

```r
o1 <- paste(capture.output(print(boxx(""))), collapse = "\n")
o2 <- capture_output(print(boxx("")))
Encoding(o1)
#> [1] "latin1"
Encoding(o2)
#> [1] "unknown"
o1 == o2
#> [1] TRUE
expect_equal(o1, o2)
expect_match(o1, o2, fixed = TRUE)
expect_match(o2, o1, fixed = TRUE)
```

And this is new testthat. The raw representation of the output is still the same, i.e. it is `latin1`, but the output is marked as UTF-8:

```r
o3 <- capture_output(print(boxx("")))
Encoding(o3)
#> [1] "UTF-8"
stringi::stri_enc_isutf8(o3)
#> [1] FALSE
o3 == o1
#> [1] FALSE
all(charToRaw(o1) == charToRaw(o3))
[1] TRUE
```

And the check results are pretty bad, you get the same for using `expect_output()` directly, of course:

```r
expect_equal(o1, o3)
#> Error in nchar(x) : invalid multibyte string, element 1
expect_match(o1, o3, fixed = TRUE)
#> Error in grepl(regexp, act$val, perl = perl, fixed = fixed, ...) : 
#>   regular expression is invalid UTF-8
expect_match(o3, o1, fixed = TRUE)
#> Error: `o3` does not match "+------+\n¦      ¦\n¦      ¦\n¦      ¦\n+------+".
#> Actual value: "+------+\n<U+00A6>      <U+00A6>\n<U+00A6>      <U+00A6>\n<U+00A6>      #> <U+00A6>\n+------+"
#> In addition: Warning message:
#> In grepl(regexp, act$val, perl = perl, fixed = fixed, ...) :
#>   input string 1 is invalid UTF-8
```

I'll be happy to do a PR, but first we need to think about the correct solution....

title: Test with no expectation becomes a "skip" (problem for test_examples)
description:
When `testthat` runs a `test_that` with no expectations in it, the result is "Skipped." I think this behavior would preferably be "Passed", since the code was executed without error or `skip()`.

In particular, this is certainly not correct behavior for `test_examples()`, which should not be expected to have an expectation. As a result, if we can change the behavior for `test_example` or `test_examples()` at least, that would be helpful! 

Also, if we are not changing the default, is it possible that we could make the "Skip" note more informative? Something like `Skipped: No expectation found`. I found it quite confusing trying to debug why my tests were getting skipped, when they were in fact being executed but did not have an expectation. 

Thanks!

title: auto_test_package do not update helpers when a test is changed
description:
If you modify a script, all tests (and helpers) are run.
If you modify a test, only that test is run, correctly.
The problem rises if you create a helper file to extract some preprocessing from a test.

When you create the helper it is run, it contains no test, and the results are all green zeros, correctly. Next, when you return to the test function, and you remove the no more necessary code, only this test is run, but not the helper, and it rises a (wrong) error.

On the other hand, the first script you modify later provide a run of the whole test folder, helper included, and from that time on the objects are stored in the test environment, and so everything return working. The problem occurs only the first time.


example:

1. Create `foo.R` in `R/`:
```
foo <- function(x) x
```

2. Create a `test-foo.R`
```
a <- 1
expect_equal(foo(a), 1)
```
All the test pass!

3. Create `helper-foo.R` 
```
a <- 1
```
The "test" `helper-foo.R` is runned reporting no test and no erorr :-)

4. Remove assignment from `test-foo.R` which becomes simply
```
expect_equal(foo(a), 1)
```
And now the test report an error
> object 'a' not found

5. Make any modification to any script, for example, add curly braces to `foo.R`, just to save it and trig the call to the tests
```
foo <- function(x) {
    x
}
```

And everything is evaluated, and all the test passed.

6. Even if you modify `test-foo.R`, e.g.
```
expect_equal(foo(a), 1)
expect_equal(foo(a), 1)
```
And only this test is called and run, from now it passes correctly. Until you change the helper:

7. Modify `helper-foo.R`
```
a <- 2
```
The "test" `helper-foo.R` is run reporting no test and no errors

8. Modify `test-foo.R` accordingly
```
expect_equal(foo(a), 2)
```
And the test is run reporting an error:
> 'a' not equal to 2
> 1/1 mismatches
> [1] 1 - 2 == -1"


Adopting a solution like the one purposed in #376 could help.

title: Comparing named vectors, ignoring order (again)
description:
This is the same as #473. That previous issue was indirectly considered resolved by the implementation `expect_setequal`, but that's not what I had in mind. `expect_setequal` tests that two sortable vectors have the same contents, but what I had in mind was that two named vectors (including lists, which aren't generally sortable) would be tested to have the same key-value pairs.

The idea is that `a` and `b` below would be considered to be equivalent:

```R
a <- list(x="a", y=2)
b <- list(y=2, x="a")
```

But these would not:

```R
a <- list(x="a", y=2)
c <- list(x="a", z=2)
```

It was closed before because @hadley thought that doing it well would require quite a bit of code, but I don't think that's necessarily true -- I had a basic implementation of it in the previous issue.

title: Update documentation: expect_s3_class returns false for base types (list, matrix, etc)
description:

Lists and matrices are S3 objects, thus I expect `expect_s3_class(myList, "list")` to pass. In fact, `class(myList)` returns `"list"`. Instead, this function returns "Error: `myList` is not an S3 object". I understand now that I should be using `expect_type(myList, "list")` instead, but this is not made clear from the help file for `inheritance-expectations`.  I understand that this gets at the minutiae of the differences between "types" and "classes" in R, but this is nonetheless confusing.

Please update the help file and examples to mention that `expect_s3_class()` is not appropriate for checking base R types, especially because the example in this help file uses the older `expect_is(a, "matrix")` syntax to test if an object is a matrix, instead of `expect_type(a, "matrix)` per the recommendation in Details.

title: as.expectation.logical() missing message in case of failure for testthat >=2.0
description:
This might be related to issue #693 

For testing our packages we are double checking the message from `as.expectation.logical` and printing it out by

```r
rec <- 2
exp <- 2
expect_equal(
  rec,
  exp,
  message=glue("Expect equal: \"Received\":\"{rec}\", \"Expected\":\"{exp}\"")
)
```
and basically parse the information given in the message to show it to the users in a test report. We can create a table with the info:

```r
data.frame(
   success  = "expectation_success" %in% class(expec),
   received = stringr::str_extract(expec$message,"(?<=Received\"\\:\")[^\\,]*(?=\\\")")
   expected = stringr::str_extract(expec$message,"(?<=Expected\"\\:\")[^\\,]*(?=\\\")")
)
>success  received expected
>   TRUE        2        2
```

This went great in testthat <2.0. Now the expect `as.expectation.logical` destroys the message in case of success.

```r
as.expectation.logical <- function(x, message, ..., srcref = NULL, info = NULL) {
  type <- if (x) "success" else "failure"
  message <- if (x) "success" else add_info(message, info)
  expectation(type, message, srcref = srcref)
}
```

we just receive
```
>success  received expected
>   TRUE      ""       ""
```

Could you plugin an option into the API to always give the failure message? Or is there a way to put our message anywhere else, e.g. into `srcref`?

A proposal by the [RTest ](https://github.com/zappingseb/RTest)team is to provide an option such as `allMessages`:

```r
as.expectation.logical <- function(x, message, ..., srcref = NULL, info = NULL) {
  type <- if (x) "success" else "failure"
  message <- if (x && !getOption("allMessages", default = FALSE)) "success" else add_info(message, info)
  expectation(type, message, srcref = srcref)
}
```

title: Enable `expect_*()` to directly compare values of expressions?
description:
The new `expect_*()` assertions enquote expressions before comparing their values. However, it is still useful to retain the ability to compare the values directly, _without_ going through enquoting.

I've encountered two scenarios where being able to fallback to the previous behavior would be useful:

1. **Circumvent an unquoting bug** (cf. https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/issues/280)
    ```R
    x <- pairlist(0)
    expect_equal(quos(UQS(x), y), quos(0, y))
    expect_equal(quos(!!! x, y), quos(0, y))
    #> Error: quos(0, y, y) not equal to quos(0, y).
    #> Length mismatch: comparison on first 2 components 
    ```
   The problem is that, currently, unquoting may produce undesirable side-effects (mutation of `x` in this case). One way to work around this is to directly compare the value of the expression of the objects, e.g., by assigning values, say, `obj1 <- quos(UQS(x), y)`, `obj2 <- quos(!!! x, y)` and then comparing `obj1` and `obj2` to `quos(0, y)`.

2. **Allow literal unquoting** (cf. https://github.com/tidyverse/rlang/issues/264)

    For example, the following assertion fails,
    ```R    
    foo <- function(x) bar(UQ(x))
    expect_equal(foo, function(x) bar(UQ(x)))
    #> Error in function (x)  : object 'x' not found 
    ```
    because the `UQ()` in the function body of the expectation is being interpreted. However, what is actually intended here is a comparison to the _value_ of the expression. One can work around this with
    ```R    
    expect_equal(foo, UQ(quote(function(x) bar(UQ(x)))))
    ```
   If `expect_equal()` had the option to compare values of (raw) expressions, then such contortions could be avoided—the _semantics_ of the assertion would be more transparently articulated.

Admittedly, these examples are rather contrived. Nonetheless, they accurately reflect the spurious incompatibilities between the tests in [nofrills](https://github.com/egnha/nofrills) and the current devel testthat.

I can resolve these incompatibilities with an _ad hoc_ wrapper:
```R
expect_equal_ <- function(object, expected, ...) {
  force(object)
  force(expected)
  expect_equal(object, expected, ...)
}
```
While this works for my purposes, a more robust alternative within testthat would be preferable. (Perhaps for a future release, if I am the only one having this problem en route to 2.0.0.)

title: all_equal() does not pass `check.name` parameters to all.equal.character()
description:
According to the documentation, `expect_equal()` will pass on parameters to `all.equal()`. Therefore, `expect_equal()` should ignore names in `target` and `current`, when passing `check.names = FALSE`. This happens for logical and numeric vectors, but not for character vectors. 

Reproduceable code

```R
library(testthat)
all.equal(c(a = "a"), "a", check.names = FALSE) #TRUE
expect_equal(c(a = "a"), "a", check.names = FALSE) 
# Error: c(a = "a") not equal to "a".
# names for target but not for current
all.equal(c(a = TRUE), TRUE, check.names = FALSE) # TRUE
expect_equal(c(a = TRUE), TRUE, check.names = FALSE) # Passes
all.equal(c(a = 1), 1, check.names = FALSE) #TRUE
expect_equal(c(a = 1), 1, check.names = FALSE) #passes
```

title: expect_equal() fails for numeric vectors containing Inf values

`

produces the error:

`
Error in is.character(message) : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed
`

This should probably be fixed by handling `Inf` values explicitly in the function `vector_equal_tol()`, making the result consistent with a call to `vector_equal()`. Alternatively, `mismatch_numeric()` could be altered, so that it handles a `diff` argument containing entries which are neither `TRUE` nor `FALSE`.

[expect_equal_inf_bug.txt](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/files/2276437/expect_equal_inf_bug.txt)

title: expect_output doesn't let you control console width
description:
Unlike `expect_known_output()`, which lets you pass a [`width` argument](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/0dbb49c883fe99c7256f357dc50be7d631f8dd1d/R/expect-known.R#L46), `expect_output()` has a hard-coded 80-character width. Even though `capture_output()` does take a width arg, `expect_output()` calls `quasi_capture()`, which calls `capture_output()` with no additional args, so you can't pass it through. 

Here's a test that illustrates:

```
context("debug")
test_that("expect_output respects 'width'", {
    withr::local_options(list(width = 10))
    expect_equal(getOption("width"), 10)
    expect_output(
        expect_equal(getOption("width"), 10),
        NA
    )
})
```

The width check inside of `expect_output` fails:

```
debug: .1.

══ Failed ══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
── 1. Failure: expect_output respects 'width' (@test-debug.R#5)  ───────────────
getOption("width") not equal to 10.
1/1 mismatches
[1] 80 - 10 == 70
```

I'm happy to submit a patch if you can provide guidance on where you'd like it solved. My instinct would be to move the `withr::local_options` setting from where it is inside [`eval_with_output`](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/0dbb49c883fe99c7256f357dc50be7d631f8dd1d/R/capture-output.R#L43) to `test_file()` or somewhere higher so that you can control print width options within your test files normally using `options(width = whatever)`. You could also extend `expect_output` to have a width argument to match `expect_known_output`, but I suspect that's a bigger refactor.

```r
tmpf <- test_temp_file()
```

```r
Error in defer(unlink(mget(new, envir = envir)), envir = envir) :

```

The testthat function could just ignore these calls.

Happy to do a PR.

title: Likely an incorrect usage of Sys.timezone on R-devel and issues on SOLARIS
description:
Lubridate runs 55 minutes on SOLARIS due to excessive use of Sys.timezone in testthat (identified by Prof Brian Ripley). 

AFAICS  testthat's [compare.POSIXt code](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/master/R/compare-time.R#L29-L31) is not using `Sys.timezone` as intended (at least not in R-devel). R-devel news states:

> ‘Sys.timezone()’ on a Unix-alike caches the value at first use in a session: _inter alia_ this means that setting ‘TZ’ later in the session affects only the _current_ time zone and not the _system_ one. 

This means that `Sys.timezone` is system time zone and not the current time-zone implied by `""`  `tzone` attribute. For example:

```R
> Sys.setenv(TZ = "America/New_York")
> Sys.timezone()
[1] "Europe/Amsterdam"
> (tt <- now(""))
[1] "2018-02-02 10:33:34 EST"
> attr(tt, "tzone")
[1] ""
```

Also setting `Sys.setenv(TZ="")` results in an unpredictable system dependent behavior. Currently there is no way to get the time zone which R uses when `tzone` attribute is "". This seems to be the intent of testthat's snippet referenced above. 

----

Here are relevant parts from my CRAN submission regarding  SOLARIS issues. The following tracebacks appear if Sys.timezone is instrumented to break before reaching to "cmp".

```R

── 1. Error: int_start and int_end work as expected (@test-intervals.R#193)  ───
Sys.timezone reached last gasp
1: expect_equal(int_start(int1), time1) at testthat/test-intervals.R:193
2: compare(act$val, exp$val, ...)
3: compare.POSIXt(act$val, exp$val, ...)
4: standardise_tzone(as.POSIXct(x))
5: identical(attr(x, "tzone"), Sys.timezone())
6: Sys.timezone()
7: stop("Sys.timezone reached last gasp")

── 2. Error: addition handles daylight savings time (@test-ops-addition.R#7)  ──
Sys.timezone reached last gasp
1: expect_that(x + days(1), equals(as.POSIXct("2010-03-15 00:00:00", tz = "America/New_York"))) at testthat/test-ops-addition.R:7
2: condition(object)
3: expect_equal(x, expected, ..., expected.label = label)
4: compare(act$val, exp$val, ...)
5: compare.POSIXt(act$val, exp$val, ...)
6: standardise_tzone(as.POSIXct(x))
7: identical(attr(x, "tzone"), Sys.timezone())
8: Sys.timezone()
9: stop("Sys.timezone reached last gasp")

── 3. Error: subtraction handles daylight savings time (@test-ops-addition.R#16)
Sys.timezone reached last gasp
1: expect_that(x - days(1), equals(as.POSIXct("2010-03-14 00:00:00", tz = "America/New_York"))) at testthat/test-ops-addition.R:16
2: condition(object)
3: expect_equal(x, expected, ..., expected.label = label)
4: compare(act$val, exp$val, ...)
5: compare.POSIXt(act$val, exp$val, ...)
6: standardise_tzone(as.POSIXct(x))
7: identical(attr(x, "tzone"), Sys.timezone())
8: Sys.timezone()
9: stop("Sys.timezone reached last gasp")
```

Judging from Prof Ripley's comment this part should never be reached unless TZ is unset:

```
>> It seems it is running 'cmp' repeatedly, so I suspect something wrong with your
>> use of Sys.timezone (on Solaris TZ should always be set, and is on the check
>> farm, so that part of Sys.timezone should never be used).
```

So I am puzzled of why Sys.timezone ends in `cmp` in the first place.

title: expect_known_value default for update param
description:
I've been using `expect_equal_to_reference` extensively for a long time and have also written a testing framework that specializes in these reference value comparisons ([`unitizer`](https://github.com/brodieG/unitizer)).  So I say the following as someone who has a lot of cycles doing tests with stored objects:

Based on my experience I think setting `update=TRUE` as the default for `expect_known_value` is sub-optimal.  The `git diff` base workflow suggested in the documentation will not work because the reference values are stored as RDS files.  `expect_known_output` is okay with `update=TRUE` because you can actually do a diff there.

Given that the `git diff` method doesn't work with RDSes, the workflow becomes:

1. Run test_check() or some such, see failures
2. Run interactively to actually look at the objects
3. Realize that you've over-written your reference objects
4. git checkout your reference objects
5. etc.

I realize the appeal of defaulting to `update=TRUE` because when the changes to values are intended, the update process is a pain when `update` defaults to FALSE.  Maybe a possibility is to have options `testthat.update.value` and `testthat.update.output` that are set to FALSE and TRUE respectively by default, and use those as the default values for `expect_known_value` and `expect_known_output` respectively?

PS: I guess I could add a [git versioned RDS comparison to `diffobj`](https://github.com/brodieG/diffobj/issues/110) since that can already compare `rds` files.

title: Idea: use as arg-checker
description:
It occurred to me that many of the checks I'd use as arg-checking code at the beginnings of exported functions might be the same things I'd use as `expect_*` functions in unit tests.  Is this a use case you've thought about?  It would be nice to get all the semantics of the expectation functions, and their more readable error messages.  In general unit test libraries tend to be a bit more feature-rich and have smoother interfaces than arg-checking libraries.  And it would be nice to have a unified model for both.

I don't like to go overboard with arg-checking, but for some high-level entry points (e.g. R code that we expose in Java APIs) it helps us fail fast when arg shapes aren't aligned, or aren't [coercible to] the right class, etc.

It probably wouldn't really make sense to actually do `library(testthat)` in application code, but a simple repackaging of the same functions into an arg-checking package could be cool.

title: Suppression of JIT compilation within testthat environments
description:
This may be intentional behaviour (or perhaps a bug with **compiler** rather than **testthat**), but just-in-time compilation seems to be suppressed when code is executed by **testthat**.

---

#### System info:
**R** 3.4.3, 3.5.0
**testthat** 2.0.0
Windows, RHEL6 and 7

#### Example: `test-jit.R`
```r
context("Use of JIT compilation within testthat")

test_that("JIT compilation", {
  
  # Define a function
  collatz <- function(k, iters) {
    
    for (i in seq_len(iters)) {
      if (k %% 2 == 0) {
        k <- k/2
      } else {
        k <- 3*k + 1
      }
    }
    
    k
  }
  
  # No JIT compilation
  compiler::enableJIT(0)
  disabled <- system.time(collatz(77031, 1000000))
  
  
  # With JIT compilation (collatz() is a closure, so any level above 0 is fine)
  compiler::enableJIT(3)
  enabled <- system.time(collatz(77031, 1000000))
  
  print(disabled)
  print(enabled)
  
  expect_lt(enabled["user.self"], disabled["user.self"])
  expect_lt(enabled["elapsed"], disabled["elapsed"])
})
```

Running the contents of the `test_that()` block line-by-line yields, with reasonable consistency on my machine:
```
> print(disabled)
   user  system elapsed 
   1.38    0.02    1.49 
> print(enabled)
   user  system elapsed 
   0.40    0.00    0.41 
```

Running the `test_that()` block as a whole yields, again with reasonable consistency:
```
   user  system elapsed 
   1.44    0.02    1.50 
   user  system elapsed 
   1.46    0.02    1.49 
Error: Test failed: 'JIT compilation'
Not expected: enabled["user.self"] is not less than disabled["user.self"]. Difference: -0.02.
```

`test_file("test-jit.R")` produces the latter result, regardless of whether the function definition/execution/timing occurs within or before the `test_that()` block.

---

Having quickly tested on another version of R I have lying around, this does _not_ appear to be an issue on R 3.2.5 with **testthat** 1.0.2 - i.e. compiled code executes more quickly, as expected.

title: expect_equal documentation unclear
description:
I find that the documentation for `expect_equal` is unclear. In a nutshell my argument is that `expect_equal` often works in complex ways that are not at all intuitively clear. This complexity if twofold: 

1. `all.equal` itself works in complex ways that are poorly documented
2. `expect_equal` is not a simple application of `all.equal`. Sometimes it does something distinctly different.

All this is best illustrated with some examples.

**Example 1**
The first difficulty is that `all.equal` itself works in complex ways. (This example is based on [stackoverflow](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/15334701/how-does-the-tolerance-parameter-of-all-equal-work).) `all.equal` can test for equality in different ways: if `target` is greater than `tolerance` it will use a relative error, but if `target` is smaller or equal to `tolerance` is will use an absolute error:
```
# The check performed by all.equal depends on which is larger: tolerance or target
all.equal(0.01, 4, tolerance = 0.01) # uses mean absolute difference
all.equal(0.01, 4, tolerance = 0.00999) # uses mean relative difference
```
This behaviour is mentioned only very briefly in the details of that function. The arguments section for `all.equal` simply states "tolerance - numeric ≥ 0. Differences smaller than tolerance are not reported. The default value is close to 1.5e-8." which seems to (incorrectly!) imply absolute differences are always used.

My issue here is that `all.equal` at least mentions this in the output of the function (it mentions whether it used an absolute or relative difference). `expect_equal` returns an output which makes no mention of the fact that an entirely different algorithm was used.
```
expect_equal(0.01, 4, tolerance = 0.01)
expect_equal(0.01, 4, tolerance = 0.00999)
```

**Example 2**
`expect_equal` sometimes does not even do the same thing as `all.equal`: 
```
all.equal(.51, .24, tolerance = 0.5) # this reports: "Mean relative difference: 0.5294118"
expect_equal(.51, .24, tolerance = 0.5) # this does not throw an error
```
Unless I'm missing something here, this is a discrepancy between `all.equal` and `expect_equal`. Again this is undocumented.

**Example 3**
It gets even more complicated when using vectors of multiple elements. The output of `expect_equal` seems to imply an element wise comparison of elements is performed, and all differences larger than `tolerance` are reported. This is not the case. `all.equal` uses a _mean_ difference (absolute or relative, see example 1). Moreover, this mean is not calculated across all elements, but only those elements that are not NA, and for which `target` is not exactly equal to `current`. Again this leads to very non-intuitive behaviour.
```
all.equal(c(10, 1e15), c(0, 1e15)) # 1e15 is eliminated because exactly equal in both cases
all.equal(c(10, 1e15), c(0, 1e15 + 1)) # A small difference (some noise?) changes this
```
This means that the errors that are reported depend not only on an element wise comparison but also on other elements in both vectors. `expect_equal` has the same behaviour.
```
expect_equal(c(10, 1e15), c(0, 1e15))
expect_equal(c(10, 1e15), c(0, 1e15 + 1))
```
Whether an element in vector `object` at index `i` is to be deemed equal or unequal to its counterpart in `expected`, depends not only on those two elements at index `i` but on all other elements of both vectors! Again this fact is obscured by the fact that `expect_equal` seems to imply element wise comparison in its output.

If a difference of 10 seems irrelevant compared to 1e15, then consider the following:
```
all.equal(c(10, 1000), c(0, 1000), tolerance = 0.5) # not equal
all.equal(c(10, 1000), c(0, 1001), tolerance = 0.5) # equal
expect_equal(c(10, 1000), c(0, 1000), tolerance = 0.5) # not equal
expect_equal(c(10, 1000), c(0, 1001), tolerance = 0.5) # equal
```

**Suggestion**
At the very least please expand the documentation for `expect_equal`.

- Highlight these problems clearly with examples
- Clearly mention that either absolute or relative difference may be used, depending on input
- Clearly mention that `expect_equal` is _not_ an element wise comparison, but uses a mean over all elements
- Highlight how and where `expect_equal` works differently from `all.equal` and why

I think many users (myself included) will automatically assume that that `expect_equal` does an element wise comparison, and then throws an error if at least one difference is larger than `tolerance`. As was shown above, this is not at all the case. Finding this out is currently not easy, and requires in-depth knowledge of the underlying function `all.equal`.

(If I may be so bold I would like to politely add that, given its complexity, the `expect_equal` function is, in my personal opinion, not at all intuitive in its current form. Even extensive documentation will not change that. As it is the aim of the `testthat` package to make testing easy and intuitive, might I suggest changing it so that it does not use the very non-intuitive `all.equal` function? I think something simple is enough: just an element-wise comparison of elements where an error is thrown if any difference is larger than `tolerance`. Perhaps an argument `relativeDifference = FALSE` could be added. This is but a humble suggestion. I will settle for clear documentation ;-).)

title: expect_identical() doesn't dispatch on identical() methods defined in other packages
description:
The core comparison within `expect_identical()` is carried out by calling `identical(x, y)` ([code link](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/expect-equality.R#L107)).

Currently, since `identical()` is not a generic, `expect_identical()` always calls `base::identical()`. However, user might want to define some specific `identical()` method for specific objects. For instance, `RProtoBuf` package defines an `identical()` method for comparing two `Message`s ([code link](https://github.com/eddelbuettel/rprotobuf/blob/master/R/identical.R#L3)). Those user-defined methods are not visible to `testthat` and are not used (see [this issue](https://github.com/eddelbuettel/rprotobuf/issues/55) in `RProtoBuf` repo for context).

It would be great if `testthat` can define a generic on top of `identical()` so that it can dispatch to specific methods defined by other packages.

title: expect_failure with multiple expectations
description:
When calling `expect_failure` with an expression that executes multiple `expect()` in a row then only the first of these expectations is evaluated. It would be useful to have an `expect_failure`-like function that evaluates all of `expr` to check for failures. This would make it possible to evaluate test functions that test complicated requirements with many successive `expect_*` calls.

Example:
```r
> testfun <- function(x) { expect_gt(x, 0) ; expect_lt(x, 1) }
> testfun(2)
Error: `x` is not strictly less than 1. Difference: 1
> expect_failure(testfun(2))
Error: Expectation did not fail
```

title: Inconsistency in test script naming conventions
description: In the help for `test_dir`, it states that test files start with "test", and this is backed up by the code in `find_test_scripts`. On the other hand, the `filter` argument is only applied once the string "test-" (with hyphen) is stripped from the filename. This could potentially lead to issues if a script is named "testfoo.R" or "test_foo.R".

title: Object comparison is painfully unhelpful
description:
First a prelude so this doesn’t come over wrong: I love testthat, life would be much much harder. Thank you. I’ve been happy to see it improve a lot over the years!

However, one part always stayed kinda lacking: Object comparison is  `expect_identical` and friends. E.g. If I pass in two vectors, with one lacking an element somewhere, `expect_identical` just tells me that the lengths are different, not which element(s) is/are actually missing/superfluous.

I found the diffobj library and wrote a quick replacement just to get a goo string diff, which works *really* beautifully (diffobj has more functions for other data types):

```r
expect_no_diff <- function(object, expected) {
    one_element <- length(object) == 1L && length(expected) == 1L
    if (one_element) {  # if we pass a 1-element string vector with '\n's
        object   <- strsplit(object,   '\n')[[1]]
        expected <- strsplit(expected, '\n')[[1]]
    }
    dif <- diffobj::diffChr(
        object, expected,
        format = 'ansi256',  # should probably be set depending on checks testthat already does
        ignore.white.space = FALSE,  # the docs say FALSE is the default but that’s a lie
        interactive = FALSE)  # necessary, else a pager plops up
    expect(!any(dif), as.character(dif))
}
```

It would be very useful to have that in testthat by default, the current output is leagues behind pytest and friends. This is the result. Note how it adapts to the width of the RStudio test output panel!

![grafik](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/291575/53985909-1beec280-411d-11e9-8793-da1766b58531.png)

title: Support for setup and cleanup
description:
This issue has been discussed a few times before (#544 is the best example), but I really think it needs more discussion. I'm currently working on a package which uses `sparklyr`. In order to test my functions I must open a Spark connection. There are three ways that I can see to do this at the moment:

1. Include a `sparklyr::spark_connect()` command at the start of each test script and a `sparklyr::spark_disconnect()` at the end. 
2. Include a `sparklyr::spark_connect()` in a `helper-00_open_connection.R` file and a `sparklyr::spark_disconnect()` in a `test-99_close_connection.R` file (note 99 represents the last test number).
3. Write a wrapper function around `testthat::test_package()` which would open a connection, run `testthat::test_package()` and then close the connection.

The first method is tedious and requires potentially opening up a lot of connections. The second method is what I am currently using - it works fine but the naming convention isn't particularly nice. The third method isn't ideal for using testing platforms like Travis (plus would need testing itself presumably). 

My current file structure is along the lines of

```
├── tests
    ├── testthat
    │   ├── helper-00_open_connection.R
    │   ├── helper-01_function_1.R
    │   ├── test-01_function_1.R
    │   └── test-99_close_connection.R
    └── testthat.R
```

But it would look a lot nicer if we could have it more like:

```
├── tests
    ├── testthat
    │   ├── cleanup-01_close_connection.R
    │   ├── helper-01_function_1.R
    │   ├── setup-01_open_connection.R
    │   └── test-01_function_1.R
    └── testthat.R
```

It would be even better if we could choose names that made "cleanup" files at the bottom and "setup" at the top. It would look more logical.

title: BROKEN: auto_test_package no longer works
description:
Took a lot of debugging, but the core issue is in testthat...

### Observed behavior

```
~/dev/pds3(master*)$ Rscript -e "testthat::auto_test_package()"
Error in path.expand(path) : invalid 'path' argument
Calls: <Anonymous> ... rprojroot_find_root -> get_start_path -> normalizePath -> path.expand
Execution halted
```

### Root Cause

I'm not sure where the regression was introduced, but the problem is that currently pkgload::load_all requires a path and testthat is passing a package here https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/auto-test.R#L90
```
pkg <- devtools::as.package(pkg)
...
env <- devtools::load_all(pkg)$env
```

As a result, the eventual pathNormalize is being passed a 'package' rather than a string

Relevant code in devtools and pkgload: 

 * https://github.com/r-lib/devtools/blob/master/R/pkgload.R#L4
 * https://github.com/r-lib/pkgload/blob/master/R/load.r#L95

### Fix

I believe that changing 
```
env <- devtools::load_all(pkg)$env
```
to 
```
env <- devtools::load_all(pkg$path)$env
```
should do the trick, but this part of the ecosystem is such a maze of packages, I'm hesitant to know exactly the correct place to make a change or where the original regression occurred as testthat hasn't actually changed to break this behavior

title: Need a way to check if expect_* passed
expect_equal_to_reference default behavior changed
description:
With the transition to `expect_known`, I think there was a regression introduced with respect to [`expect_equal_to_reference` ](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/expect-known.R#L124):
```
 #' @export
-#' @rdname expect_known_value
+#' @rdname expect_known_output
 #' @usage NULL
-expect_equal_to_reference <- expect_known_value
+expect_equal_to_reference <- function(..., update = FALSE) {
+  expect_known_value(..., update = TRUE)
+}
```
Should be:
```
expect_equal_to_reference <- function(..., update = FALSE) {
  expect_known_value(..., update = update)
}
```
Happy to submit a PR if you want, but it may be easier for you guys to fix.  Let me know.  For reference, the NEWS entry suggests the change is not intentional:

> expect_known_value() replaces expect_equal_to_reference(), which has been soft-deprecated. It gains an update argument defaulting to TRUE. This changes behaviour from the previous version, and soft-deprecated expect_equal_to_reference() gets update = FALSE.

title: expect_equal gives misleading error message for equivalent objects
description:
If the actual and expected values are equivalent but not equal, then the failure message from `expect_equal` is misleading: it seems like a floating point rounding problem.

``` r
expect_equal(c(a = 1), 1)
## Error: c(a = 1) not equal to 1
## 1 - 1 == 0
```

When this expectation has failed, `all.equal` should be a character vector describing the problems.  It might be more informative to print these as well.  In this case, the output I'm suggesting would be:

```
## Error: c(a = 1) not equal to 1
## 1 - 1 == 0
## names for target but not for current
```

Very loosely related: https://github.com/hadley/testthat/issues/339

title: testthat crash (including a trivial package to reproduce)
description:
RStudio (as well as R sessions run from the terminal) crashes when devtools::test is invoked twice in succession on a package that uses Catch, via package testthat. The crash occurs in testthat/include/testthat/vendor/catch.h.

I've attached a trivial package that reproduces the problem:
[ttcrash.tar.gz](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/files/2225953/ttcrash.tar.gz)

Exact steps to reproduce:
1.) Simply install the package to "some_directory".
2.) > "library(devtools)"
3.) > test("some_directory/ttcrash")
4.) > test("some_directory/ttcrash")

The crash will occur on the last step. I'm using R version 3.4.4 and testthat version 2.0.0

title: Adding test_that_file() function

```r
#' Create the path to a test that file

testthat_file <- function(...) {
  file.path(rprojroot::find_testthat_root_file(), ...)
}
```

title: Can't detach package in tests
description:

```
context('whatever')

test_that('some tests where I detach my package', {
  detach(package:packagefileprob, unload = TRUE, force = TRUE)
  expect_error(bar())
  expect_silent(packagefileprob::bar())
  library(packagefileprob)

library(clipr)

test_that('some tests where I detach a different package', {
  detach(package:clipr, unload = TRUE, force = TRUE)
  expect_error(dr_clipr())
  expect_error(clipr::dr_clipr(), NA)
  library(packagefileprob)
})

```

From the command line the `test_that` call runs silently. But if I run `devtools::test()`, I get:

```
test-detach.R:6: failure: some tests where I detach my package
`bar()` did not throw an error.
```

This matters if I want to write tests that ensure my package works when called without being attached.

The second testthat chunk works fine. Only the package being tested cannot be detached.

`detach()` seems to fail silently. The `unload` and `force` arguments don't make a difference.

title: Scoping Issue within Test
description:
With the same test run manually vs. through test_dir, the result changes.

I have a function, business below, that when I run the test manually, it works without issue.  When I run it automatically with test_dir, it fails.  I think that it's a scoping issue with the formula evaluation, but I can't seem to isolate the problem.

Specifically, here is the function and the pair of tests:

```
business <- function(FUN,
                     zero.missing=FALSE,
                     max.missing=0.5)
  function(x, ...) {
    ## Allow functional input instead of numeric/logical
    if (inherits(zero.missing, "formula"))
      zero.missing <- eval(zero.missing[[2]])
    if (inherits(max.missing, "formula"))
      max.missing <- eval(max.missing[[2]])
    mask.missing <- is.na(x) | (zero.missing & (x %in% 0))
    if (sum(mask.missing)/length(x) > max.missing)
      return(NA)
    FUN(x[!mask.missing], ...)
  }
```

Tests:

```
test_that("business", {
  choice <- function() TRUE

  expect_equal(b.mean.3(c(0, 1)), 1)
```

title: Ability to run come set up code across all tests
description:
This is pretty much what was asked in issue [544](https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/issues/544)

As outlined in that issue, we have some common machine environment set up commands that need to run exactly once before all tests defined in the package. However, we only want these to be run in the context of running our unit tests.

Creating a helper.R file in the tests/testthat does work however it appears to have a side effect:  the lines in the helper file also executed when we build the documentation as part of a Makefile target, which calls 
R -e 'devtools::document(pkg="mypackage", roclets=c("namespace", "rd"))

So on our target production machine even though we are not running any unit tests, when we build & install our package with the Makefile, it ends up running those commands in helper.R

Is there a different way to accomplish this? Or are there parameters to the document method I can pass in, to not have it source the helper file?

Thanks.

title: ProgressReporter overwrites previously printed lines in RTVS terminal
description:

Maybe something in the inherited `self$cat_tight(...)` or `end_context(...)` in [reporter-progress.R](../blob/master/R/reporter-progress.R) is causing this issue.
`sink`ed to a file results show all updates line-by-line (in my case of a hundred of light tests - one line per each passed test)

At [this commit](https://github.com/njtierney/naniar/commit/bf72c1322bc48634794ab55aca6de6864e5ae584) of naniar I get the following print message when I run devtools::test()

(apologies for hard coding the pkg PATH in the reprex, I couldn't get it to work otherwise!

The problem is that it doesn't print that I have 5 tests that failed, but shows me that I have 5 tests that failed.

When I run `devtools::check()` I can identify that the tests all fail in test-replace-with-na-where.

Perhaps I've missed something obvious, but thought you might like to know about this,

Thanks again for building and maintaining a package I use every day!

title: helper file sourced twice
description:
Hi, the helper-file is sourced twiced. As I test creation and manipulation of folders this causes problems - although I found a workaround. See [here](https://stackoverflow.com/q/47350561/5784831). 

A stand-alone example can be found [here](https://github.com/Christoph999/test/tree/master/tests)

I would be happy if anybody could solve the problem or explain the behaviour. Thanks in advance, Christoph

title: build (including roxygen) runs testthat?
description:
The build of my package creates folders unintentionally. I tried to solve the problem (see [here](https://stackoverflow.com/q/47491656/5784831)), but wihout success. 

I created an example [here](https://github.com/Christoph999/test/tree/master/tests). The tests run fine (folder created and deleted) but when I build the package, the folder is created but not deleted.
Why is it built at all? If that is on pupose: Why is it not deleted by the ZZ-test-file?

Help is highly appreciated - I couldn't find a workaround for that! I hve no clue, how to further track down that issue...

title: test_that does not search for S3 methods the same as its calling environment
description:
This is the same issue as #266 (with an updated title).

`test_that` does not search for the same S3 methods as its calling environment.  If the S3 method is defined within `test_that`, it is not found when running the test.  (The issue could also be in expect_equal-- mainly, the code below should work.)

``` r
library(testthat)
foo <- function(obj) UseMethod("foo")

foo2 <- function(obj) {
  foo(obj)
}

test_that("foo2 fails", {
  foo.character <- function(obj) {
    paste(obj, obj)
  }
  expect_equal(foo2("hi"), "hi hi")
})
#> Error: Test failed: 'foo2 fails'
#> * no applicable method for 'foo' applied to an object of class "character"
#> 1: expect_equal(foo2("hi"), "hi hi") at <text>:12
#> 2: compare(object, expected, ...)
#> 3: foo2("hi")
#> 4: foo(obj) at <text>:5
```
``` r
library(testthat)
foo <- function(obj) UseMethod("foo")

foo2 <- function(obj) {
  foo(obj)
}

# foo2 has the expected result

  paste(obj, obj)
}
foo2("hi")
#> [1] "hi hi"
```

title: Add warnings are errors option
description:
From @jimhester [here](https://community.rstudio.com/t/fail-ci-on-warnings-in-tests/6187/9):

> What you would likely want to do is modify https://github.com/r-lib/testthat/blob/master/R/reporter-check.R to additionally tally expectation_warning and then stop for warnings in a similar way to how it stops for errors.

> But maybe at this point it would be better to open an issue in the testthat repository and we can consider adding a stop_for_warning option to the check reporter.

title: Add skip_if_offline()
docs: improve documentation for code consumers
description:
I have just needed to use testthat as a consumer of a package tested by testthat. The package provides a wealth of documentation for authors for use in testing their code, but there is not (I possible I just can't find) a simple and introduction and use vignette for consumer users wanting to run the tests on a package.

As a user of someone else's code, I'd like to be able to do `library(pkg); library(testthat); test_package("pkg")`. Reducing the friction on this particular action is what wold make people generally more inclined to randomly test packages and for that user behaviour to become ingrained, but finding that set of commands took more effort than I would have expected. When I tried it (and other permutations I was not successful in getting the tests to run) - see https://github.com/openjournals/joss-reviews/issues/593#issuecomment-375323491 (I posted `test_package("pkg")` but had also tried `test_package(pkg)`).

I'm coming from a Go background where the build chains testing infrastructure can be invoked from any location, e.g. `go test package/path/identifier`. Which was my understanding for the behaviour of `test_package`.

The author of that package has hooked travis to do the build, so I don't need to run them locally now. Related to this, is there an option to verbosely output the names of package tests that have been run (e.g. [from a set of our tests](https://travis-ci.org/gonum/gonum/jobs/357065778#L578))?

Apologies for the ramble. Hopefully I have made my concern clear enough.

title: expect_error does not return caught errors
description:
From `?expect_error`:

> If expect_error() captures an error, that is returned instead of the value.

In fact it always returns NULL on an error:

```
res <- expect_error(stop("foo"), "foo")
res
# NULL
res <- expect_error(stop("foo"))
res
# NULL
res <- expect_error(stop("foo"), NA)
Error: `stop("foo")` threw an error.
Message: foo
Class:   simpleError/error/condition
res
# NULL
```

title: cat_line namespace error - maybe require cli >= 1.0.0 ?
description:
I just ran into a strange namespace issue. (Sorry, no good MWE). I'll suggest that testthat depends on the 'cli' package version >= 1.0.0.

I had been running testthat 1.2.0, and I used install.packages() to update to testthat 2.0.0. Then, I ran:
```
> testthat::test_file(
+   path = ftt,
+   reporter = "minimal"
+ )
Error: 'cat_line' is not an exported object from 'namespace:cli'
```
Similarly and unsurprisingly, running `devtools::test()` from the Rstudio hotkeys:
```
==> devtools::test()

Loading mypkg
Loading required package: testthat
Testing mypkg
Error: 'cat_line' is not an exported object from 'namespace:cli'
In addition: Warning message:
package 'testthat' was built under R version 3.3.3 
Execution halted
```

I saw that I had cli version 0.0.0.9000 installed. I didn't check to see what commit, or when it had been installed. 

#### Installing cli v1.0.0 from CRAN fixed the above issue.


- Perhaps change testthat to depend on cli >=1.0.0? It worked for me.
- I looked through the [GH history](https://github.com/r-lib/cli/blob/master/R/cat.R) of the cli package, and it seems that `cat_line()` has had `@export` in the roxygen docs since Hadley first added the function. I'm stumped.

title: Run tests only once in CI (e.g. Travis) setting with covr enabled
description:
As far as I understand, in a typical CI setting, e.g. on Travis, all tests are run twice, once during `R CMD check` and once again during `covr::codecov()`. This seems wasteful. Wouldn't it make more sense, to skip testing during checking and instead have covr fail if a test fails? Is this currently possible?

I'm sorry if this has been discussed somewhere before - I couldn't find anything on the topic.

title: enhancement: extend test_example to validate output
description:
Currently, `test_examples()` does no more than `R CMD check`. If the developer has copied "*pkg*.Rcheck/*pkg*-Ex.Rout" from a previous run to "tests/Examples/*pkg*-Ex.Rout.save", then `test_examples()` in fact does less.

Twice (#335 and #255) it has been suggested that testthat could improve on `R CMD check` by individually validating Rd examples. I'm adding a third vote for this enhancement. If it remains outisde the scope of testthat, is there an alternative package where this feature could be welcome?

If a PR would be considered, please offer any additional guidance that would be critical for its adoption.

title: Adding `wrap` Parameter to `test_dir`, `test_check`, and `run_tests`
description:
@krlmlr, Since 37cc0d04 it is no longer possible to run code with `test_dir` that involves `withCallingHandlers` error handling.  This is because the default source action now sets [`wrap=TRUE`](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/master/R/source.R#L15), which causes all sourced code to be run within [`test_code`](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/master/R/source.R#L31).

Since `wrap` is not exposed in [`test_dir`](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/master/R/source.R#L31) there is no way to disable this behavior when using `test_dir` (or `test_check`).

A simple example of the problem (here we just use `test_file` since `test_file` has the argument so we can show both cases):
```
f <- tempfile()
cat(
  "
  withCallingHandlers(
    stop('This should be handled'),
    error=function(e) cat('handled\n')
  )
  test_that('truth', {expect_true(TRUE)})
  ",
  file=f
)
test_file(f)              # fails
test_file(f, wrap=FALSE)  # works
```
For reference, more details on the running [`withCallingHandlers` inside `try` block issue](http://stackoverflow.com/questions/20572288/capture-arbitrary-conditions-with-withcallinghandlers).

I'm happy to submit a PR that addresses this if you'd like.

title: Why are `expect_` functions all titled with questions?
description:
Hello! I have the above, maybe naive, maybe language question about the docu for all the `expect_` functions (for example [`expect_equal`: `Expectation: is the object equal to a value?`](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/master/R/expect-equality.R#L1)). Doesn't an expectation imply that something _is_, not whether it might be this or that? I'm not a native English speaker, though! Maybe I am missing an obvious rationale for using `?`here?

I started using `testthat` regularly through [Exercism.io's R track](https://github.com/exercism/r) and am sometimes confused by the report about a failed test. Sometimes, there are `x[1]: ` and `y[1]: ` listed with some results, or `Lengths differ: … vs …`, and it's not clear which is the expected and which is the actual result. OTOH `… not equal to …` in a report makes it perfectly clear :-)

Thus, as an occasional testthat user, I wondered how the output or the docu could be updated in order to improve the understanding of reports about failed tests. I feel motivated to work on rewording the titles, in order to specify which expectation exactly needs to be met in order to make test pass. In case of `expect_equal` for example: `Expectation: The object is equal to a value.`.

Would that be a useful contribution here?

title: Use warning() for "warnings" instead of cat()
description:
First of all, thank you to everyone working on this package! I find it very useful.

I prefer to turn warnings into errors. (related discussion:
http://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/Turn-warnings-or-notes-into-errors-on-CMD-check-td4698214.html)

However, testthat does not use R's warning mechanism for the warnings it prints. I think it would be better to rely on R's centralized warning mechanism than catting the string "warning".

More details:

R CMD check currently gives me:

```
[cut]
* checking tests ...
  Running ‘test_no_loess_warnings.R’
  Running ‘test_smoother_stuff.R’
  Running ‘testthat.R’
  Running ‘testz_smoother_output.R’
[cut]
```

As you can see, there is no warning in the output here. However, testthat does give warnings (see the output at the bottom for the specific warnings given).

If I inspect the created testthat.Rout file, I could see the warnings. But I do not want to manually set up a grep.

testthat could either use the `warning()` function for each warning. Or it could use cat but at least at the end use the `warning()` function once, such as `warning("there were warnings")`.

If testthat does not want to use R's warnings for some reason, perhaps it could just use a different word (to me, a "warning" is well-defined in R), or perhaps respect conventions such as the "warn" option. For example, the warn option is ignored in the following:


title: change expect_silent to include object output
description:
(This is softly mentioned #614, and related to it since I'm trying to replace `info` functionality.)

I want to test for silence (or warning or error) from a function and still test its output. If a function is "expensive", I'd much rather not run it multiple times. However, the current `expect_silent` and family explicitly discard the object upon execution.

Right now I can do

```r
expect_silent2 <- function(obj) { expect_silent(o <- obj) ; o ; }
```

but this does not work using the NSE hack for replacing `info`. That is:

```r
expect_silent(myfunc(FALSE))
expect_silent(myfunc(TRUE))
# Error: myfunc(TRUE) produced warnings.
expect_silent2(myfunc(FALSE))
# [1] FALSE
expect_silent2(myfunc(TRUE))
# Error: o <- obj produced warnings.
```

That last error message isn't very useful, so I try the NSE trick:

```r
expect_silent3 <- function(obj) { eval(bquote(expect_silent(.(o <- obj)))) ; o ; }
expect_silent3(myfunc(TRUE))
# Warning in myfunc(TRUE) : quux
# [1] TRUE

expect_silent4 <- function(obj) { eval(bquote(expect_silent(o <- .(obj)))) ; o ; }
expect_silent4(myfunc(TRUE))
# Warning in myfunc(TRUE) : quux
# [1] TRUE

expect_silent5 <- function(obj) eval(bquote(expect_silent2(.(obj))))
expect_silent5(myfunc(TRUE))
# Warning in myfunc(TRUE) : quux
# [1] TRUE
```

but none of them triggers the `Error: myfunc(TRUE) produced warnings` I would expect.

title: Unwrapped Tests Not Reported
description:
With the introduction of the `wrap` argument to `test_file`, tests outside of `test_that` are processed as tests, but they are not actually recorded:
```
> test_file('tests/testthat/test_dir/test-bare-expectations.R', wrap=TRUE)
Bare: ..

DONE ===========================================================================
> .Last.value
data frame with 0 columns and 0 rows
```
This appears to happen because `test_code` explicitly does not start or end tests for NULL tests, which is what is used for the `expect_` calls that aren't within `test_that` blocks.  One possible fix is:
```
diff --git a/R/source.R b/R/source.R
index afc7bcd..73e96b7 100644
--- a/R/source.R
+++ b/R/source.R
@@ -28,7 +28,7 @@ source_file <- function(path, env = test_env(), chdir = TRUE,
     on.exit(setwd(old_dir), add = TRUE)
   }
   if (wrap) {
-    invisible(test_code(NULL, exprs, env))
+    invisible(test_code("(unknown)", exprs, env))
   } else {
     invisible(eval(exprs, env))
   }
```
After which:
```
> test_file('tests/testthat/test_dir/test-bare-expectations.R', wrap=TRUE)
Bare: ..

DONE ===========================================================================
> .Last.value
                      file context      test nb failed skipped error warning
1 test-bare-expectations.R    Bare (unknown)  2      0   FALSE FALSE       0
   user system  real
1 0.006      0 0.006
```
This change does break a few other tests, which I haven't looked into:
```

length(res) not equal to 4.
1/1 mismatches
[1] 5 - 4 == 1

`df` not equal to reference from `test_dir.rds`.
Attributes: < Component “row.names”: Numeric: lengths (24, 17) differ >
Component “file”: Lengths (24, 17) differ (string compare on first 17)
Component “file”: 11 string mismatches
Component “context”: Lengths (24, 17) differ (string compare on first 17)

Component “test”: Lengths (24, 17) differ (string compare on first 17)
Component “test”: 17 string mismatches
Component “nb”: Numeric: lengths (24, 17) differ
Component “failed”: Numeric: lengths (24, 17) differ
...
```
I can look into a PR for this if you'd like, but would appreciate some feedback before I spend time trying to figure this out.

title: undoc'd string length limitation on NSE replacement for 'info'
description:
I believe you are considering (or actively) deprecating the `info` argument to many `expect` functions. I understand the value of using NSE for `label`, but it has a length limitation I'm butting my head against.

**Working example:** a function that takes an input file, does something to it (silently), and returns a `data.frame`. Because the processing is non-trivial, I want to do it only once per file, so I capture the return value after testing for silence (ergo `expect_silence2`). I need to run it twice on each file (diff arguments).

Taking a cue from your [tests chapter](http://r-pkgs.had.co.nz/tests.html#test-tests), I believe a way to do this is something like:

```r
my_complex_function <- function(fn, add1 = FALSE) data.frame(x = seq_len(nchar(fn)) + add1)
expect_silent2 <- function(obj) { expect_silent(o <- obj) ; o ; }
expect_mytests <- function(fn) {
  out0 <- expect_silent2(my_complex_function(fn, add1 = FALSE))
  out1 <- expect_silent2(my_complex_function(fn, add1 = TRUE))
  nr <- function(a, b) nrow(b)
  eval(bquote(expect_lt(nr(.(fn), out0), 10)))
  eval(bquote(expect_lt(nr(.(fn), out1), 10)))
}
```

Ideally, I'd run it as `for (fn in allfiles) expect_mytests(fn)`, but for the sake of this issue:

```r
expect_mytests(strrep("b", 9))
expect_mytests(strrep("b", 53))
# Error: nr("bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb", out0) is not strictly less than 10. Difference: 43
expect_mytests(strrep("b", 54))
# Error: nr(...) is not strictly less than 10. Difference: 89
```

First: we've lost the NSE info on the last call (not dependent on `options("width")`). Filenames can be (and in my use, "are often") over 53 characters, and this complete loss is unexpected. I can strategically truncate the string, though this is prone to "works best for me" syndrome (e.g., first 50? last 50? first/last 25?).

Second: the only way I can imagine providing that file-specificity with the failure messages is to add it as an unused argument to my `nr` function. This works, but it seems a bit kludgy. Is this the only way to include the filename (in this example) within the failure message?

(Third: is this really the best/only way to get the `info` stuff into the failure message?)

As I'm writing this ... if I switch the order of the arguments within `nr`, this goes away:

```r
expect_mytests <- function(fn) {
  out0 <- expect_silent2(my_complex_function(fn, add1 = FALSE))
  out1 <- expect_silent2(my_complex_function(fn, add1 = TRUE))
  nr <- function(a, ...) nrow(a) # arguably better-looking, anyway
  eval(bquote(expect_lt(nr(out0, .(fn)), 10)))
  eval(bquote(expect_lt(nr(out1, .(fn)), 10)))
}
expect_mytests(strrep("b", 99))
# Error: nr(out0, "bbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbbb") is not strictly less than 10. Difference: 89
```

Is this a limitation of `eval` or `bquote`, or is this something `testthat` is imposing? (I could not find "54" ...)

Related issue refs:

- #218 Deprecate label & info arguments
- #332 Add info, label arguments to expect_silent
- #360 Use conditions for reporting results
- #392 consider un-deprecating `info` (and `label`?) for certain expectations
- #429 expect_silent missing info field?
- #476 expect_{lt,gt} don't have 'info' argument

title: Test hanging in R CMD check but not when run interactively
description:
I have recently started using testthat to unit test our ``PharmacoGx`` Bioconductor package, and I have run into an issue with the expect_equal_to_reference test. This following code in testing our package runs interactively (using both devtools::check() and check_package()), but when called by R CMD check hangs indefinitely (R stops using any CPU resources for upwards of half hour, must be interrupted to continue check with errors due to interruption):
```
library(PharmacoGx)
require(parallel)
context("Checking intersectPSet.")

test_that("Intersection result did not change since last time", {
	data(GDSCsmall)
	data(CCLEsmall)
	expect_equal_to_reference(intersectPSet(list('GDSC'=GDSCsmall, 'CCLE'=CCLEsmall), intersectOn = c("drugs", "cell.lines","concentrations")), "intersectedSmallData.rds")
})
```
I have narrowed down the issue to specifically the setting of the parameter: `` intersectOn = c("drugs", "cell.lines","concentrations")``, with the setting `` intersectOn = c("drugs", "cell.lines")`` working properly in both cases.

The main difference is that when concentrations is included in the list, the code calls a function (``PharmacoGx:::.calculateSensitivitiesStar``) which relies on ``makeCluster``  and ``parSapply`` from the parallel package. ``makeCluster`` is called with 1 as the parameter, and this same code (``intersectPSet(list('GDSC'=GDSCsmall, 'CCLE'=CCLEsmall), intersectOn = c("drugs", "cell.lines","concentrations"))`` runs fine as part of the documentation examples when run by R CMD check. 

Given that I cannot reproduce this issue interactively, I am having trouble probing the issue and creating a more minimal working example. Maybe someone with more knowledge of the exact environment in which R CMD check runs the tests can help me reproduce the issue in an R session?

title: expect_equal, no tol=? expect-failure testing
description:
I encountered a bug when something should've failed which did not in my own code.
I was trying to use `expect_equal` with a `tol=` arg, and I changed something which should've flunked an expectation.

I looked into the test-set for this package, and it seems there is no **expect-failure** for two objects failing the tolerance criterion. Testing this myself, it seems sometimes it works, but there are edge cases for which it behaves as it clearly should not.

Examples:

`expect_equal(3000,3001)` #> Fails, as it should.  

`expect_equal(3000, 3001, tol = 2)` #> passes, as it should.  

`expect_equal(3000, 4000, tol = 0.1)` #> Fails, as it should.  

`expect_equal(3000, 3001, tol = 0.1)` #> **PASSES, for which it should NOT**.
--> (Falls outside the tolerance window)

`expect_equal(3000, 3001, tol = 0.1, scale = 1)` #> Fails, back to intended behavior.  

`expect_equal(3000, 3001, tol = 0.1, scale = NULL)` #> PASSES, for which *I believe* it should not.  

Unless there are tests for the equality set elsewhere, it looks like this bug would've fallen-through development since there are no tests in its associated test-file which test for **failing tolerance intervals:**






https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/master/tests/testthat/test-expect-equality.R
