title: suggested function: fake_tribble
description:
**Up front:** I have already written this. Is this interesting enough for me to submit a PR? I'd rather not write tests and documentation if it does not interest you.

I find myself maintaining a static `data.frame`; for many reasons, I prefer to keep it as a textual representation, not as a `rdata` file, a `csv`, or anything similar (though the latter could be used with similar utility). The use of `tribble` is quite nice for this: it is both easily *readable* and easily *manually edited*, much more so than traditional `data.frame`s. However, they are not so easily appended en masse. If I need to add 10 rows, to continue using `tribble`, I would need to type everything manually or do a bit of cut/paste and string-handling (fairly manual).

In comes my suggested function: `fake_tribble()`.

```r
fake_tribble(iris) %>% print(n=5)
# tibble::tribble(
#     ~Sepal.Length, ~Sepal.Width, ~Petal.Length, ~Petal.Width, ~Species    
#   ,           5.1,          3.5,           1.4,          0.2, "setosa"    
#   ,           4.9,            3,           1.4,          0.2, "setosa"    
#   ,           4.7,          3.2,           1.3,          0.2, "setosa"    
#   ,           4.6,          3.1,           1.5,          0.2, "setosa"    
#   ,             5,          3.6,           1.4,          0.2, "setosa"    
# # ... with 145 more rows
# )
```

I can now easily copy just the relevant lines and insert into an already-started static `tribble` definition (that is, just copy the text of the rows I need and insert/append).

This is completely a utility function; it requires no external dependencies (not even the existence of `tribble`) to create the textual representation.

Some useful characteristics of this utility:

- `class`ed: using `print.fake_tribble`, it allows easy console use (`cat`) for copying while maintaining the `character` vector internally; it similarly supports console-truncation as demonstrated above
- it is row-wise independent; by using the prepended comma (a stylistic preference, admittedly), it facilitates easily dealing with individual data rows without worrying about first/last
- it is code-wise complete, meaning `eval(parse(text = fake_tribble(iris)))` works as one might expect
- it allows some customization such as custom indentation

(If there's an already-existing function that handles this, I missed it.)

The formals, if you are curious:

```r
fake_tribble <- function(x, max_width = NA, collapse = ", ", compact = FALSE) { ... }
print.fake_tribble <- function(x, ..., indent = 2, n = 50, sep = "\n") { ... }
```

title: Add support to mark tests as known failures
description:
A common TDD workflow is to add a "known failing" test as soon as a bug is reported, and then remove the "known failing" annotation once the bug is fixed. To support this workflow, `testthat` could say add a parameter `known.failure` or `warn.on.failure` as in
```
test_that("Bug #1234", known.failure = "TODO(fritzo)", {
   # Run the example provided in bug report.
   ...
})
```
This feature is useful when you have thousands of tests some small percent of which are know to fail, and a single cleanup commit may fix 5 tests but break 2 others.

Note that this FR is distinct from `expect_failure` which annotates a single expectation, rather than a test with multiple expectations.

title: `format.mismatch_character` produces warning  and erroneous output when there are many differences
description:
An example:

```
> library(testthat)
Warning message:
package ‘testthat’ was built under R version 3.2.5 
> expect_equal(letters[1:6], LETTERS[1:6])
Error: letters[1:6] not equal to LETTERS[1:6].
6/6 mismatches
x[1]: "a"
y[1]: "A"

x[2]: "b"
y[2]: "B"

x[3]: "c"
y[3]: "C"

x[4]: "d"
y[4]: "D"

x[5]: "e"
y[5]: "E"

x[6]: "a"
y[6]: "A"

1: In mapply(FUN = f, ..., SIMPLIFY = FALSE) :
  longer argument not a multiple of length of shorter
2: In mapply(FUN = f, ..., SIMPLIFY = FALSE) :
  longer argument not a multiple of length of shorter
```

Notice that in addition to the warnings, the first 5 elements of the two vectors are being recycled (see `x[6]` and `y[6]`).

The problem is in [`format.mismatch_character`](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/a102b89a8f23120ea5e614a1adf229b947e14850/R/compare-character.R#L83), where anytime there are more differences than `max_diffs` (currently defaults to 5), `show_x`, `show_y`, and `x$i` are no longer the same lengths in the [`Map` call](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/a102b89a8f23120ea5e614a1adf229b947e14850/R/compare-character.R#L93).

Let me know if you want me to submit a PR to fix this, assuming you agree with what I laid out above.

title: testthat_results is empty with test_dir
compare() reports attribute differences even with check.attributes=FALSE
description:
Here's an example:

```
> x <- 1:5; y <- x+0.2; attr(x, "thing") <- "value"
> compare(x, y, check.attributes=FALSE)
Attributes: < Modes: list, NULL >
Attributes: < Lengths: 1, 0 >
Attributes: < names for target but not for current >
Attributes: < current is not list-like >
```

Internally, this is because `compare()` (and thus all the functions that use it, like `expect_that()` and friends) first calls `all.equal()` to determine whether the comparison passes or fails - but then if it fails, it tries to reconstruct why it failed, but does so incorrectly.

One fix would be to check whether `list(...)` contains `check.attributes` with a `FALSE` value, and if so, skip the attribute reporting.

title: Comparing named vectors, ignoring order
description:
It would be useful to have an expectation that compares two named vectors (or environments) and returns TRUE if all the named items are the same, regardless of order. Currently, to do this you need to sort the items by name before comparing. For example:

``` R
# Return TRUE if any items in vector x are unnamed; FALSE otherwise.
any_unnamed <- function(x) {
  # Zero-length vector
  if (length(x) == 0) return(FALSE)

  # List with no name attribute
  if (is.null(names(x))) return(TRUE)

  # List with name attribute; check for any ""
  any(!nzchar(names(x)))
}

sort_by_name <- function(x) {
  if (any_unnamed(x)) 
    stop("Can't sort by name because there are unnamed items")

  if (any(duplicated(names(x))))
    stop("Can't sort by name because there are duplicate names")

  x[sort(names(x))]
}


a <- list(x=1, y=2)
b <- list(y=2, x=1)

expect_identical(sort_by_name(a), sort_by_name(b))
```

It would be nice to be able to do something like this:

``` R
expect_identical_contents(a, b)
```

(The function name could be better though.)

title: Piping to and from output expectations
description:
Hi there,

I am wondering how the pipe symbol %>% is supposed to behave with output expectations. Note that piping is entirely omitted from the PDF documentation of testthat version 1.0.2 . Hence, the only thing I know about piping is what I read on https://blog.rstudio.org/2016/04/29/testthat-1-0-0/ .

*\* Use case of output expectation piping**
I would have liked to write something like this:

```
sqrt(4) %>% expect_error(NA) %>% expect_equal(2.0)
```

Obviously, if sqrt() generated an error, it would not make sense to then call expect_equal(). However, here, I expect no error and would like to pipe to test additional things.

**Piping in problem**
A potential problem is that using the piping syntax, sqrt() is evaluated fist, and then passed to expect_error(). Thus, we loose the capability of expect_error() to run tryCatch() to capture any error message like it is done when issuing expect_error(sqrt(4),NA) directly.

**Piping out problem**
invisible(NULL) is returned from expect_error(), expect_warning() and expect_message(), which prevents them from piping to other downstream expectations. One should perhaps consider returning something better to allow piping out. At the very least, I suggest mentionning in the documentation that these expectations cannot pipe to other expectations.

Cheers!

Florent

title: Expose test_code
description:

title: expect_named to allow extra column names
description:
## Use case

You need a data.frame that has _at a minimum_ a certain set of columns; others are allowed and silently ignored.

**Suggestion**: add argument `ignore.extra` (or something similar), default to `FALSE`.
## Example

``` r
x <- mtcars
testthat::expect_named(x, c("cyl", "vs"))
# Error: Names of `x` ('mpg', 'cyl', 'disp', 'hp', 'drat', 'wt', 'qsec', 'vs', 'am', 'gear', 'carb') don't match 'cyl', 'vs'
testthat::expect_named(x, c("cyl", "vs"), ignore.extra = TRUE)
# (no error)
```

Currently can do the following, with the error message on failure:

``` r
testthat::expect_length(setdiff(c("cyl", "vsOOPS"), colnames(x)), 0)
# Error: setdiff(c("cyl", "vsOOPS"), colnames(x)) has length 1, not length 0.
testthat::expect_identical(setdiff(c("cyl", "vsOOPS"), names(x)), character(0))
# Error: setdiff(c("cyl", "vsOOPS"), names(x)) not identical to character(0).
# Lengths differ: 1 vs 0

# this errors before testthat sees it
testthat::expect_named(x[,c("cyl","vsOOPS")], c("cyl", "vsOOPS"))
# Error in `[.data.frame`(x, , c("cyl", "vsOOPS")) : 
#   undefined columns selected
```

... but the errors are slightly under-informing. I would hope for an error message such as:

``` r
testthat::expect_named(mtcars, c("cyl", "vsOOPS"), ignore.extra = TRUE)
# Error: Names of `x` ('mpg', 'cyl', 'disp', 'hp', 'drat', 'wt', 'qsec', 'vs', 'am', 'gear', 'carb') don't contain 'cyl', 'vsOOPS'
```

title: Support to run test setup/cleanup?

```R
context("test")

safeVar <- "OK to put this here?"

test_that("need safeVar 1", { //... })

```

title: [Request] assert_that function that's appropriate for use within a function
description:
Currently, if I try to use ``expect*`` within functions I get funny behavior with ``expect_error`` when trying to violate the expectation in the function:

```
square_root <- function(x){
  testthat::expect_gte(x, 0)
  sqrt(x)
}

expect_error(square_root(-1))
# Error: -1 is not more than 0. Difference: -1 

square_root <- function(x){
  stopifnot(x >= 0)
  sqrt(x)
}

expect_error(square_root(-1))
# works
```

``assertthat`` works as well, but development on that package seems to have stalled. Is it possible to add an ``assert_that`` function to ``testthat`` that would work like this:

```
square_root <- function(x){
  testthat::assert_that("x input is positive", {
    expect_gte(x, 0)
  })
  sqrt(x)
}

expect_error(square_root(-1))
# would work
```
``assert_that`` would somehow make the error behavior from ``expect*`` functions work like ``stopifnot``.

title: warnings not converted to errors with warn=2 in tests
description:
create an empty package with this test file:

```
test_that('warning bug', expect_error({options(warn = 2); warning('toto')}) )
```

with the current HEAD version of testthat, you get:

```
1. Failure(@test-testhat_bug.R#1): warning bug ---------------------------------
{
    options(warn = 2)
    warning("toto")
} code did not generate an error
```

I tracked it down to commit 5ffe62f9441b3e03c801032908479945d4e651df , which makes sense.

I tried to fix it, but it does not seem trivial. 
But I wonder: is it really a good idea to silence the messages and warnings in the tests ? 
I mean, there are too cases: 
- expected warnings, that the test author is aware of. In that case he can explicitly suppress them using suppressMessages and suppressWarnings around the expect_xxx() calls.
- non expected warnings. If you silence them, you could hide bugs in the tests code. 

What do you think ?

title: using test_that with Jenkins (fork)
description:
G'day Hadley

I'm wanting to get test_that reports into a form that can be understood by Jenkins (http://www.jenkins-ci.org/). Basically that means the jUnit XML format -- Jenkins will highlight failing tests, giving options for more detail, show timing of groups of tests, overall trends etc. 

So I went ahead and wrote a JUnitReporter at https://github.com/floybix/test_that

One problem was the need to identify tests stably over time even though they may start failing. For that I am using the deparsed expect_that() call itself. Currently it works to my satisfaction with expect_that() but not with expect_equals() etc. 

Also the invocation is a little awkward to redirect to a file... output goes to standard out by default so in the ideal case where nothing else gets printed one could simply

```
sink("testjunit.xml")
test_package("testthat", reporter = "jUnit")
sink()
```

But the safer option is something like

```
test_package("testthat", reporter = JUnitReporter$clone()$do(self$file <- "testjunit.xml"))
```

What do you think?

```
f = function() {
    options(warn = 2)
    result = NULL
    result = tryCatch(

    )
```

```
    })
```

title: Calling `test_dir` inside of `test_that` can silently fail
description:
While working on https://github.com/hadley/testthat/pull/467, I noticed that the expectations in test-reporter-tap.R weren't being evaluated. Pulling the `test_dir` outside of the `test_that` block made the expectations run (and fail). I did a little more investigation, and I found a few things:

A. Running this:

```
context("test_dir inside test_that")

test_that("testing the test_dir", {
  test_dir("test_dir", reporter="tap")
  expect_true(FALSE)
})
```

yields

```
test_dir inside test_that: 1..2
# Context Bare
ok 1 testing the test_dir
not ok 2 testing the test_dir
  attempt to apply non-function
  1: test_dir("test_dir", reporter = "tap") at testthat/test-test-dir.R:9
  2: test_files(paths, reporter = reporter, env = env, ...)
  3: with_reporter(reporter = current_reporter, results <- lapply(paths, test_file, env = env, 
         reporter = current_reporter, start_end_reporter = FALSE, load_helpers = FALSE))
  4: force(code)
  5: lapply(paths, test_file, env = env, reporter = current_reporter, start_end_reporter = FALSE, 
         load_helpers = FALSE)
  6: FUN(X[[i]], ...)
  7: with_reporter(reporter = reporter, start_end_reporter = start_end_reporter, {
         lister$start_file(basename(path))
         source_file(path, new.env(parent = env), chdir = TRUE)
         end_context()
     })
  8: force(code)
  9: source_file(path, new.env(parent = env), chdir = TRUE)
  10: eval(exprs, env)
  11: eval(expr, envir, enclos)
  12: expect_that(1, equals(1)) at test_dir/test-bare-expectations.R:3
  13: condition(object)
  14: expect_equal(x, expected, ..., expected.label = label)
  15: expect(comp$equal, sprintf("%s not equal to %s.\n%s", lab_act, lab_exp, comp$message), 
         info = info)
  16: withRestarts(if (expectation_broken(exp)) {
         stop(exp)
     } else {
         signalCondition(exp)
     }, continue_test = function(e) NULL)
  17: withOneRestart(expr, restarts[[1L]])
  18: doWithOneRestart(return(expr), restart)
  19: signalCondition(exp)
  20: (function (e) 
     {
         register_expectation(e, frame + 11, sys.nframe() - 6)
         invokeRestart("continue_test")
     })(structure(list(message = "1 not equal to 1.\nEqual\n", srcref = NULL), .Names = c("message", 
     "srcref"), class = c("expectation_success", "expectation", "condition")))
  21: register_expectation(e, frame + 11, sys.nframe() - 6)
  22: get_reporter()$add_result(context = get_reporter()$.context, test = test, result = e)
  23: o_apply(self$reporters, "add_result", context = context, test = test, result = result)
  24: lapply(objects, function(x) x[[method]](...))
  25: FUN(X[[i]], ...)
  26: x[[method]](...)
```

All of the tests in "test_dir" were not run, and the `expect_true(FALSE)` was not hit either. And the contents of the TAP output from the test_dir call are contaminated by the description of the `test_that` that encloses it.

B. Wrapping `test_dir` in `capture.output` prevents the failure but skips further execution. This was why the expectations in test-reporter-tap.R weren't running but weren't failing like above.

Executing this

```
context("test_dir inside test_that")

test_that("testing the test_dir", {
  output <- capture.output(test_dir("test_dir", reporter="tap"))
  expect_true(FALSE)
})
```

shows no expectations running at all, including no `FALSE isn't true.` I saw https://github.com/hadley/testthat/issues/460 and wondered if it was potentially related.

C. Running the existing tests for `test_dir` in https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/master/tests/testthat/test-test_dir.R, I see only two expectations passing. It appears that the first test block bails out before L34 runs, but the other two expectations are executed, as confirmed by adding `expect_true(FALSE)` after all three and seeing which failed. So it appears that there are conditions under which test_dir can be called successfully from inside test_that.

title: run all tests then stop on error?
description:
It seems like a function to run all the tests and then stop if there's an error would be pretty helpful. The reporter `stop` stops on error, and the default behavior runs all the test, but there's nothing I see that conveniently combines them.

It's only a few lines of code for a user:

```
results <- devtools::test(".")
results_df <- data.frame(results)
if (any(results_df$failed | results_df$error)) {
  stop(sprintf("Failed: %s, Error: %s", sum(results_df$failed), sum(results_df$error)))
}
```

But this seems common enough (for example, it's almost always what you want on a CI server) that a helper function or a reporter for it might be good.

title: auto_test_package keeps printing failure messages of passing tests that failed previously
description:
The watcher (`auto_test_package`) seems to be holding onto failure messages even after the tests pass again. With a toy package and file "tests/testthat/test-something.R", containing:

```
context("A test")

test_that("true is true", {
    expect_true(TRUE)
})
```

I fired up R and started watching:

```
$ R
> library(testthat)
> auto_test_package("../testpackage/")
Loading testpackage
A test: .

DONE ===========================================================================
```

title: expect_success and expect_failure defunct
description:
As far as I understand the documentation, this should work:

``` r
expect_success(expectation("success", message = "foo"))
expect_failure(expectation("failure", message = "foo"))
```

Problem is probably here: https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/master/R/expect-self-test.R#L45 where you return `NULL` instead of the expectation.

title: test_equal for POSIXt uses very low tolerance and ignores `tolerance` argument
description:
Two issues. 

First, the tolerance for timedates beyond milisecons is not very reasonable for R.  For example lubridate has a simple computation of `decimal_date` and `date_decimal` which naturally looses in precision. Here is the crux of it:

``` r
> start <- ymd("2012-01-01")
> now <-  ymd("2012-03-01")
> end <- ymd("2013-01-01")
> 
> sofar <- as.numeric(difftime(now, start, units = "secs"))
> total <- as.numeric(difftime(end, start, units = "secs"))
> dec <- 2012 + sofar/total
> 
> now2 <- start + (dec - 2012) * total
> expect_equal(now, now2)
Error: `now` not equal to `now2`.
1/1 mismatches
[1] 2012-03-01 - 2012-03-01 00:00:00 == -3.34e-06 secs

```

So by adding and subtracting 2012 you get e-06 difference due to multiplication with large POSIX number (`total`).

Second problem is that `tolerance` argument is ignored for POSIXt objects:

``` r
> expect_equal(now, now2, tolerance = 1)
Error: `now` not equal to `now2`.
1/1 mismatches
[1] 2012-03-01 - 2012-03-01 00:00:00 == -3.34e-06 secs
```

title: `doesnt` as alternative to `not` to avoid magrittr name conflict
description:
I find that I have to write testthat::not pretty often, as I may have loaded testthat before magrittr. Can I suggest adding an alias to `not` called `doesnt`. It's not perfect, having the punctuation omitted, and the grammar of `doesnt(throws_error(...` makes me wince, but this could also be aliased to `throw_error`. `does_not` might be better.

This is not just cosmetic, as I have spent time debugging tests where I used plain `not` and `magrittr::not` confused `testthat`.

title: Autorun Examples as Tests
description:
Would it be possible to add a feature to run documentation examples as tests?  I'd love to write the examples once in a way that best-helps the user understand the code, but the simple "does it give an error" check that happens during `R CMD check` doesn't give assurance that the test worked.

It separates the tests into two locations (bad) but it is a write-once solution (good).  Feel free to tell me that this doesn't align with the plans for testthat.

I initially asked this question on stackoverflow for roxygen2, but thinking more, it seems like a devtools feature (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/34080889/can-i-automatically-generate-unit-tests-for-testthat-from-roxygen2-examples).

title: Guaranteed order of a sequence of tests in a package
description:
In certain applications it is important to have a precise and guaranteed order of tests. For example, the test that is doing "test data import" should be done before the test that is verifying "the consistency of imported data".

It looks like the key function here is [`find_test_scripts`](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/6cdd17cab674175297e16e12ac5ed29266534390/R/test-files.r#L76) which does not seems to guarantee a particular order of files. (does `dir` guarantee the same sort order across different platforms?)

Does it make sense to return `sort(files)` instead of [`files`](https://github.com/hadley/testthat/blob/6cdd17cab674175297e16e12ac5ed29266534390/R/test-files.r#L91) in order to make sure that the order of tests is deterministic and predictable? or does `dir` already do that in a cross-platform-safe manner?

title: Allow matching multiple lines of output in expect_output
description:
For testing functions that write content to a file, the easiest to way to test them is (I think) to write to stdout and check that the lines of output are what you expected.  This avoids any worries about write permissions and cleaning up afterwards.

Currently `expect_output` only allows you to match a single regexp so you have to have a test like:

``` r
test_that(
  "my_write_fn write to stdout",
  {
    expected <- c("line1", "line2")
    actual <- capture.output(my_write_fn(some_input)) 
    expect_equal(actual, expected)
  }
)
```

I think it would be more natural if you could write a test like:

``` r
test_that(
  "my_write_fn write to stdout",
  {
    expected <- c("line1", "line2")
    expect_output(my_write_fn(some_input), expected)
  }
)
```

title: Negation of tests
description:
For "old-style expectations", there is `not()` -- e.g., `expect_that(object, not(is_null(...)))`: http://stackoverflow.com/a/30037495/946850. I'm not aware of a way to achieve this with the "new style". How about the following syntax:

```
n(expect_null)(object)
```

The package could also define

```
nexpect_null <- n(expect_null)
```

(same for all other functions).

At the core is the function `nexpect_that()` which is `expect_that()` with a negated condition. The function `n()` would be implemented by substituting `expect_that` with `nexpect_that` in the body.

title: using vector `class` argument in `expect_is` causes errors in `test_dir`
description:
##### TL;DR: When calling `test_dir` on a test containing an `expect_is` call with character vector `class` argument, two errors are reported, causing an error in a `vapply` call before ever reporting the failures.

`expect_is` mangles the error message slightly when the `class` argument is a vector:

``` r
x <- NA
class(x) <- c('a')
expect_is(x, c('b', 'c'))
```

`Error: x inherits from a not bx inherits from a not c`

which isn't so bad, but when used in test_dir (and quite possibly others) it leads to the following cryptic error:

``` r
dir <- tempdir()
write("test_that('blah',{
         x <- NA
         class(x) <- c('a')
         expect_is(x, c('b', 'c'))
       })",
      file = paste0(dir, '/test-demo.R'))
test_dir(dir)
```

`Error in vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) { : values must be length 1, but FUN(X[[1]]) result is length 2`

The error is thrown by the following line in `test_dir`:

``` r
current_reporter$end_reporter()
```

because `failure_summary` returns a vector of length two mangling the `vapply` call

```
[1] "1. Failure (at test-demo.R#4): blah -----------------------------------------\nx inherits from a not b"
[2] "1. Failure (at test-demo.R#4): blah -----------------------------------------\nx inherits from a not c"
```

Hope this is helpful!

title: expect_equals(a,b,0.01) silently ignores 0.01 from v0.10.1
description:
v0.9.1  :  expected behaviour

```
> expect_equal(415, 416, 0.01)
> expect_equal(415, 416, tolerance=0.01)
```

v0.10.0   May 2015,  currently on CRAN

```
> expect_equal(415, 416, 0.01)   # 0.01 silently not passed on to all.equal, apparently
Error: 415 not equal to 416
416 - 415 == 1
> expect_equal(415, 416, tolerance=0.01)   # tolerance= now required.
```

We all know we should always name our arguments. Anyone who hasn't may now be bitten by this when they upgrade. It's the silent apparent ignoring of the 3rd argument that's confusing.  `?expect_equals` contains `... = other values passed to all.equal`   and when you then look at `?all.equal` it seems reasonable to assume the 3rd argument matches up with the 3rd argument of `all.equal` (i.e. `tolerance`).

A few solutions I can think of are i) restoring previous behaviour, ii) catch and warn/error about any unnamed arguments or iii) add to `?expect_equals` that `tolerance` must now be explicitly named.

description:
```

Not expected: as.character(5) not equal to 5
Modes: numeric, character. Not expected: as.character(5) not equal to 5
target is numeric, current is character. 
```

From what I tracked down, there are several problems:
1. the "worst" one is that failures don't get cleaned up in the reporter if the function `end_test()` throws an error, which prevents further use of the package. A quick fix would be to flush it first.
Then, either:
2. `format.expectation` (called by `as.character`) should collapse the several `failure_msg` of the expectation.
3. Only one `failure_msg` should be allowed.

Thanks to @jimhester for bringing this up and see https://github.com/jimhester/covr/issues/58 for more discussion of the coveralls.io use case.

title: failed <<- TRUE should be done by the Reporter base class
description:
### Reason

The member is declared and initialized in the base class, and hence should be modified (only) there.
### Implementation

All other reporters will need to `callSuper()` in `add_result()`, and probably also in `start_reporter()`.
### Use case

Different test files use different reporters, like this:

```
with_reporter(MultiReporter$new(reporters = list(get_reporter(), DetailedReporter$new())), {
...
})
```

The "main" file (e.g., `tests/testthat.R`) uses the "basic" reporter only to collect global success status:

```
test_check("tikzDevice", reporter = Reporter$new())
```

Currently I need to implement a subclass to work around this.

title: Teardown functions or files
description:
I think it would be great to have them. It might be possible to work around them, but it is getting cumbersome. Here is what I want to do for the tests:
1. Create a temporary database in a DBMS.
2. Run a bunch of tests using the temporary DB.
3. Delete the DB.

I don't think this is a very uncommon use case.
## Temporary DB within a test file

Assuming one creates the DB at the beginning of a test file, and then deletes it at the end, then it is almost fine. The glitch is that any error that happens outside of a `test_that` call will stop the parsing of the file and the teardown at the end does not run. E.g. if you test this:

``` r
cat("hello\n", file="/tmp/hello")

## Error
"a" + 10

test_that("", {
  expect_true(TRUE)
})

## Teardown
unlink("/tmp/hello")
```

with `test_file()`, then `/tmp/hello` is not removed. If you put the error within a `test_that` call, then all is fine.
## Temporary DB for all test files

Creating and destroying DBs is kind of slow and resource intensive, so ideally I would want to create one DB for all tests, spread over a number of files. Helper files are great to create the DB. Now I would need some teardown files to delete it. 

How about having `test_dir` read in and run all files that start with `teardown`, after all tests finished? (And also `on.exit()` as well, obviously.)

Am I missing something? If yes, please tell me. If not, interested in a PR to do this?

title: In-place mocking
description:
Currently, `with_mock` works by patching references to functions. This is already complicated enough (both package and namespace environments have to be patched), and does not even work for imported functions (see https://github.com/hadley/testthat/pull/169#issuecomment-56162515 and https://github.com/lbartnik/varia/pull/1).

Perhaps it's easier in the end to patch R's internal structures in place using C code.

title: Mocking
description:
Useful to test functions that normally interact with the file system or the web, such as `install_github` in `devtools`. Also to speed up integration tests that involve heavy computation.

As suggested in https://github.com/hadley/devtools/pull/475/files#r16603091 . Proof of concept is available [in `devtools`](https://github.com/krlmlr/devtools/blob/2ef4ed6dce69b96ebac3d1e7a6ef7f1243c65042/tests/testthat/test-github.r#L3), a robust implementation will perhaps add a new environment to the search path.

Was suggested before in #93. @lbartnik: Are you still interested?

Was also discussed in hadley/devtools#388. CC: @wch.

title: `expect` function
description:
There’s a proliferation of `expect_*` functions, and they’re getting more with every new test added, and I’m not entirely sure that this is actually needed.

To the best of my understanding, the general pattern of `expect_that(object, condition)` mimics testing frameworks in other languages such as Java, and is purpose is to allow accurately reporting the failed condition as a readable error message. This technique, I think, was pioneered by the [Hamcrest](http://hamcrest.org/) Java library.

… and then the `expect_*` functions are just convenience “shortcuts” for the long form which nevertheless preserve the readable failure message.

But fundamentally, the purpose of Hamcrest was to “work around” the fact that Java expressions, once compiled, cannot trivially be made into readable expressions, hence the use of a DSL of matchers.

But R doesn’t need this! It’s trivial to get an sexpr or a readable representation of an expression in R. So I’m wondering, why isn’t there simply an `expect` macro which takes a normal R expression as its sole argument? I’m probably missing something, but wouldn’t the following be much simpler and more flexible than the current approach?

``` splus
test_that('some object has the correct value', {
    expect(! is.null(some_object))
    expect(length(some_object) > 5)
})
```

Yielding

```
Failure: some object has the correct value
length(some_object) <= 5
```

This would only require getting the topmost node in the parse tree and finding its complement. At its most simple, a `switch(substitute(condition)[[1]], …)`, although of course this is simplified and probably won’t be quite enough.

But maybe there’s another purpose to using a DSL rather than native R expressions that I’m missing?

title: `source_dir` use COLLATE for load order
description:
`auto_test_package` is a wrapper for `auto_test` using package directory conventions. `auto_test` loads source from the `code_path` directory using the `source_dir` function. `source_dir` in turn loads the files in `code_path` alphabetically.

I'm working with `testthat` as a maintainer on an older package. This package uses `COLLATE` in the `DESCRIPTION` file to ensure that source files are loaded in the proper order. `COLLATE` is created using `roxygen` based on the `@include` directive in each file. Because the load order is not alphabetical, I can't use `auto_test_package` while working on this package.

It would be nice if `source_dir` could use the order from `COLLATE` (if it exists) to load source files rather than alphabetically. Even better would be if `source_dir` could use `roxygen2:::generate_collate`, but this would require 1) a dependency on Roxygen and exporting `generate_collate` or 2) duplicating this functionality in `testthat`, neither of which are particularly desirable solutions.

I'm happy to make this addition and submit as a PR. Before doing so wanted to check if this addition would be welcome and discuss implementation strategy.

title: Should testthat export more functions?
description:
I receive files from a third party each day, and I need to check them to make sure they are formatted correctly and contain reasonable values.  For example, suppose that I have a data.frame, created by reading a csv, that looks like this

```
dat <- data.frame(A=1:3, B=c("a", "b", "c"), stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
```

I want to be able to run a function and get output that looks like the output from test_package().  So, it should look like this:

```
checkMyFile(dat)
format : ....
values : .
```

---

To accomplish the above, I have a file called "check.my.file.R" in /inst/tests that has the following in it:

```
context("format")
test_that("names are as expected", {
  expect_identical(names(dat), "A", "B")
})
test_that("classes are right", {
  expect_is(dat, "data.frame")
  expect_is(dat[["A"]], "integer")
  expect_is(dat[["B"]], "character")
})

context("values")
test_that("all values in A are unique", {
  expect_true(!any(duplicated(dat[["A"]])))
})
```

That file is not run by test_package() because it does not have the word "test" in its name.

Finally, I have a function in my package that runs the tests in that file:

```
checkMyFile <- function(file, reporter="summary") {
  # create an object "dat" that will be used in /inst/tests/check.my.file.R
  dat <- if (is.character(file)) {
    read.csv(file, stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  } else if (is.data.frame(file)) {
    file
  } else stop("'file' should be a file path or a data.frame")
  reporter <- testthat:::find_reporter(reporter)
  path <- system.file("tests", "check.my.file.R", package="MyPackage")
  testthat:::with_reporter(reporter, {
    sys.source(path, new.env(parent = environment()), chdir = TRUE)
      testthat:::end_context()
  }) 
}
```

---

I've been doing this for a long time, and I'm happy with it.  However, CRAN is cracking down on using ":::".  I don't use this in any public packages, so it doesn't really matter to me, but it makes me wonder whether there is a better way to do the above, or whether find_reporter(), with_reporter(), and end_context() should be exported.

title: @templateVar in roxygen doesn't appear to work properly
description:
I'm trying to use brew templates.  Basic templates work just fine, but variables don't seem to work the way they're documented.

The docs say that I need to set variables inside the roxygen section.  So I have something like this:

```
#' @templateVar foo value
#' @template some_template
```

I set up a simple template:

```
(man-roxygen/some_template.R)
#' <%=foo%>
```

However, roxygen will complain that "foo" doesn't exist.   I tried doing an ls() inside of the template tag, and found that only templateVar exists.  So, this will work:

```
(man-roxygen/some_template.R)
#' <%=templateVar%>
```

Note that I still need to have some sort of arbitrary "foo" variable in the @templateVar directive, but they all get coerced to have the name "templateVar" in the template.

title: Additional matchers
description:
I've found the following matchers useful to highlight the intent of my expectations. If you think any of them could be useful more broadly, let me know and I'll submit a pull request.

``` R
context("MongoCollection")

test_that("local connection to test DB", { 
  subject <- MongoCollection$new(test_db(), 'test')

  expect_proto(subject, 'MongoCollection')
  expect_interface(subject, 'add', 'count', 'db', 'drop', 'find', 'find_one', 'full_name', 'insert', 'is_connected', 'name', 'remove')

  expect_true(s$is_connected())
  expect_equal(s$name(), 'test')
  expect_equal(s$full_name(), paste(DB, 'test', sep='.'))
})

test_that("CRUD", { 
  data <- list(name='sim', tags=c('founder', 'cto', 'angel'))
  coll <- MongoCollection$new(test_db(), 'test')
  coll$insert(data)

  subject <- coll$find(query = list(name = 'sim'))
  expect_length(subject, 1)

  subject <- subject[[1]]
  expect_mongo_doc(subject)
  expect_includes(subject, data)
})
```

title: Inaccurate error reporting from tests
description:
I have noticed that the error context reported by `test_that` sometimes seems inaccurate while also lacking important debugging information such as line numbers. 

Consider the following error:

``` R
1. Error: connect ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
$ operator is invalid for atomic vectors
1: AnalyticsSystem$connect()
2: get(x, envir = this, inherits = inh)(this, ...)
3: .$db()
4: get(x, envir = this, inherits = inh)(this, ...)
5: MongoDB$new(host = config$hosts, db = config$database, replica = config$set_name, username = config$username, password = config$password)
6: get(x, envir = this, inherits = inh)(this, ...)
7: mongo.create(host, replica, username, password, db, timeout)
```

It seems that the error is coming from `mongo.create` but here is the implementation from the `rmongodb` packages:

``` R
function (host = "127.0.0.1", name = "", username = "", password = "", 
    db = "admin", timeout = 0L) 
{
    mongo <- .Call(".mongo.create")
    attr(mongo, "host") <- host
    attr(mongo, "name") <- name
    attr(mongo, "username") <- username
    attr(mongo, "password") <- password
    attr(mongo, "db") <- db
    attr(mongo, "timeout") <- timeout
    .Call(".mongo.connect", mongo)
}
```

The implementation doesn't seem to use the `$` operator at all. 

Here is the implementation of the calling function:

``` R
MongoDB <- proto(
  ..Name = 'MongoDBFactory', 

  new = function(., host="127.0.0.1", replica="",
                    username="", password="", 
                    db="test", timeout=60*1000L) {

    mongo <- mongo.create(host, replica, username, password, db, timeout)
    stopifnot(mongo.is.connected(mongo))

    .$proto(
      ..Name = 'MongoDB'
      # rest of implementation 
    )
  }
)
```

What can developers do in their code to make error context more accurate? Also, can we get files & line numbers in error messages? It's the kind of thing users of a testing framework tend to rely on...

title: fail function for forcing a test failure
description:
There's been a request for a `fail` function in `testthat`, that just makes a test fail.  

http://stackoverflow.com/questions/12507229/how-to-make-a-test-fail-with-the-testthat-package

I had a go at writing one, for possible inclusion in the package.
# ' Makes a testfail
# '
# ' The fail function forces a test to fail.
# '
# ' @param message a string to display.
# ' @param infoextra information to be included in the message (useful when writing tests in loops).

fail <- function(message = "Failure has been forced.", info = NULL)
    {
      expect_that(
        NULL,
        function(message)
        {
          expectation(FALSE, message) 
        },
        info = info,
        NULL
      )
    }

Usage is, for example,

```
test_that("failure test", fail())
```

title: source() ignores environment when test_file() called on file
description:
I have a function called `do_something.r` that does something, but I want it to do something else when I'm testing it. The reason is because it does something different every day and I want to make it do something over the same time period for testing, so my test assertions can remain fixed.

I have the following block in `do_something.r` that allows it to do it's thing unless I call it in a testing mode. Testing mode is on if the `microphone` is `TRUE`

``` R
if(!exists("microphone") || !isTRUE(microphone)){
      voice = "do_something code"}
```

The rest of `do_something` is this: 

``` R
 cat("Voice is from the", voice, "\n")
```

When this file is sourced from R, we get the following result

``` R
> source('do_something.R')
Voice is from the do_something code 
```

The result we would expect. Next I wrote the `source_something.r` script to make sure my assumptions about how `source()` works were correct.

``` R
 microphone = TRUE
 voice      = "source_something code"
 source("do_something.R")
```

When `source_something.r` is itself sourced, we get the following result in R.

``` R
> source('source_something.R')
Voice is from the source_something code 
```

Now let's put the `source_something` block inside a test script called `test_something.r`

``` R
require(testthat)

microphone = TRUE
voice      = "source_something code"
source("do_something.R")
```

When this file is tested in R, we don't get the expected result

``` R
> test_file('test_something.r')
Voice is from the do_something code 
```

Somehow, the `microphone = TRUE` assignment gets lost as does (presumably) the `voice = "source_something code"` assignment when the file is run under the `testthat` framework.

Is there a work around for this I can use?

Thanks a lot,
Janko

title: convenience function for expect_that
description:
The following is a convenience function that is useful when you are working in an interactive session and you decide that you want to test one of the objects in your workspace. The function inputs the object you want to test and an argument that must be "equals", "is_equivalent_to", or "is_identical_to". It outputs the test that you can copy and paste into an R script.

``` R
export_test <- function(x, test = "equals") {
        stopifnot(test %in% c("equals","is_equivalent_to","is_identical_to"))
        substitute(expect_that(subme1,subme2(subme3)),list(subme1=substitute(x),subme2=as.name(test),subme3=x))
}
```

For example, suppose you have the following factor:

``` R
happiness <- factor(c("happy", "not at all happy", "not at all happy", "quite happy", "not very happy"))
```

If you run the following command,

```
export_test(levels(happiness),"is_identical_to")
```

You get this output:

```
expect_that(levels(happiness), is_identical_to(c("happy", "not at all happy", "not very happy", "quite happy")))
```

```
}
```

We don't really know that the 7th one fails, for instance, if something fails there. Allowing for a `message` parameter that is printed in the failure report could help to address this issue, ie:

```
for (idx in 1:length(result)) {
  expect_identical(result[[1]], expected[[1]], message=sprintf("%dth item failed", idx))
}
```

(Sorry if this isn't the right place of feature requests, please direct me elsewhere if it's not)

title: Export `expectation` class/method through the NAMESPACE
Error in str_c when using test_dir
description:
@update2
I suspect that at this stage when using test_dir you always need to use test_that, not single expect_that calls. The problem is that single test_that calls do not have a 'tests' object, which, according to the example below, returns NULL when trying to extract it and causes the error in str_c

Paul

@update1
I just found out that when I use the setup:

test_that("It is not equal", expect_that(1, equals(2))))

That the function runs fine. The following code fails when using test_dir:

expect_that(1, equals(2)))

regards,
Paul

@first message
Hi Hadley,

I've looking into unit testing and found your package. However, I ran
into some issues. I had the following testfile:

context("context 1")
expect_that(1, equals(2))
expect_that(5, equals(2))

context("context2")
expect_that(3, equals(1))

located in the subdirectory "tests". When running:

test_dir("tests")

I got the error:

test_dir("tests")

context 1 : 12
context2 : 3Error: Input to str_c should be atomic vectors

> > traceback()
> > 5: stop("Input to str_c should be atomic vectors", call. = FALSE)
> > 4: str_c(label, ". ", type, ": ", tests, " ")
> > 3: reporter$end_reporter()
> > 2: with_reporter(reporter, {
> >        source_dir(path, "^test.*\.[rR]$", env = env)
> >    })
> > 1: test_dir("tests")

I traced the problem down to the summary reporter (reporter-summary.r).
In line 65:

tests <- sapply(self$failures, "[[", "test")

the function tries to extract the "test" attribute from self$failures.
The problem is that there is no "test" attribute and returns NULL and
the line after that fails with the above mentioned error:

header <- str_c(label, ". ", type, ": ", tests, " \n")

In other reporters, failure$test is assigned the value 'desc' (e.g. in
self$start_test of reporter-stop.r), we could this in self$start_context
for reporter-summary. But I'm not really sure what the best solution is
right here. Would it be possible to fix this?

regards,
Paul

title: printed output from expectations can go wrong
description:
Long expressions in an expect_that() statement can be deparsed into multiple lines, and this messes up the printed output when it is paste()d.

Example, of a failing test:

```
expect_that(fitted(armax.sriv.fit(cbind(U = U, Q = Q_n3s3), order = c(3,0))), equals(Q_n3s3, tol = 1e-5))
# Error: Test failure: 
# fitted(armax.sriv.fit(cbind(U = U, Q = Q_n3s3), order = c(3,  not equal to Q_n3s3Test failure: 
#0))) not equal to Q_n3s3
```

The relevant deparse() statements occur in expectations.r and in expect-that.r

Perhaps something like
    name <- paste(deparse(substitute(object)), collapse = "\n")
or
    name <- paste(deparse(substitute(object), width = 500), collapse = "\n")

title: Prevent testthat from deleting snapshots created on other systems
description: I use R/Positron both on Windows and Linux. For some tests, I test visual snapshots on both system, with different variants: ```r skip_on_os(c("mac", "solaris", "windows")) skip_if_not_installed("ggplot2") skip_if_not_installed("see") skip_if_not_installed("vdiffr") skip_if_not_installed("emmeans") skip_if_not_installed("marginaleffects", minimum_version = "0.29.0") skip_on_cran() test_that("plots facets", { data(efc, package = "modelbased") # make categorical efc <- datawizard::to_factor(efc, c("c161sex", "c172code", "e16sex")) fit <- lm(neg_c_7 ~ c12hour * barthtot * c161sex * c172code, data = efc) pr <- estimate_means(fit, c("c12hour", "c172code", "c161sex")) set.seed(123) vdiffr::expect_doppelganger( "plot-interaction-facets-1", plot(pr, show_data = FALSE), variant = "linux" ) ... ``` I have the same test-file for windows, where I skip on Linux and save snapshots as windows-variant. However, on each system, snapshots that are not checked via the tests are removed by testthat. E.g., the following tests are skipped on Linux And when testing is over, I have 101 deleted SVG-files. Question (and I couldn't find anything searching the internet so far): How can I prevent testthat from removing those snapshots?

title: Hiding errors when the test records another result after it (perhaps in an exit handler)
description:
Is this intended?

Hand-written reprex, Claude's version in https://github.com/r-dbi/RSQLite/issues/837 .

``` r
library(testthat)

dir <- tempfile()
dir.create(dir)

writeLines(
  c(
    'test_that("ok", {',
    # Dropping the line below makes the test fail as expected
    '  on.exit(warning("cleanup warns"))',
    '  stop("boom")',
    "})"
  ),
  file.path(dir, "test-x.R")
)

res <- test_dir(dir, reporter = "check", stop_on_failure = TRUE)
#> Saving _problems/test-x-3.R
#> [ FAIL 1 | WARN 1 | SKIP 0 | PASS 0 ]
#> 
#> ══ Failed tests ════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
#> ── Error ('test-x.R:3:3'): ok ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> Error in `eval(code, test_env)`: boom
#> 
#> [ FAIL 1 | WARN 1 | SKIP 0 | PASS 0 ]

writeLines(readLines(file.path(dir, "_problems/test-x-3.R")))
#> # Extracted from test-x.R:3
#> 
#> # test -------------------------------------------------------------------------
#> on.exit(warning("cleanup warns"))
#> stop("boom")

as.data.frame(res)[c("test", "failed", "error", "warning")]
#>   test failed error warning
#> 1   ok      0 FALSE       1
# Expected: error = TRUE, to match FAIL 1 in the summary line above

# The error is recorded, but it is not the test's last result
lapply(res[[1]]$results, class)
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "expectation_error" "expectation"       "error"            
#> [4] "condition"        
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "expectation_warning" "expectation"         "condition"
```
